Like many lords of the early Edo period, he wanted a kiln of his own to supply tea ware for the castle and presentation gifts (kenjōhin) for the shogunate and other lords. In 1624 he invited Ōtani Sōemon (大谷宗右衛門, 1588–1659), a potter from Hizen in northern Kyushu, where climbing kilns and Korean-derived techniques had spread after the 1590s. The traditional founding date of 1624 is not universally accepted. Sōemon built a three-chamber climbing kiln on the slope of the Ninomaru, the castle's second enclosure, called the Sagimai Kiln (鷺舞窯) after the castle's nickname. Its products were not sold: they were used in the castle, given to retainers and temples such as Kōun-ji, or sent to Edo as gifts. Each piece was impressed with a small seal of crossed heron feathers, the Asagiri crest. The Ōtani family served as hereditary kiln masters for eight generations on a stipend of 30 koku and guarded their glaze recipes, which were passed on orally from father to son. The kasumi glaze appeared at the domain kiln in the mid-17th century; the earliest dated example, a tea bowl whose box carries an ink inscription of 1667, is in the Harukawa Castle keep museum. Suyama commercial kilns[edit] Private kilns appeared in Suyama village, about 12 km up the Kagami River from the castle, in the 1680s. The fourth lord, Asagiri Tadanobu (r. 1680–1712), licensed them as part of the recovery from the Tenna famine of 1681–82, the same policy that led him to order the planting of yuzu in 1688. The commercial kilns used the local iron-rich clay and were barred from using the kasumi glaze and the heron seal, which were reserved for the domain kiln. Instead they used clear ash glazes and an amber iron glaze, and stamped their wares with the character 春 (haru) in a square. They made storage jars, sake flasks, mortars and plates for townspeople and farmers. The ware went down the river on flat-bottomed boats to the merchants of Harukawa and by sea from Minori Bay to Osaka. The largest of the commercial kilns was the Suyama Old Kiln (陶山古窯), a 14-chamber communal climbing kiln built about 1690 on the hillside above the village. About 58 m long, it was shared by several kiln families, who rented chambers for each firing. A domain survey of 1838 counted 27 kiln households and about 400 workers in Suyama. The Suyama Old Kiln was fired until 1931 and became a National Historic Site on 4 October 2015. Decline and export ware[edit] The abolition of the domains in 1871 ended the domain kiln. The eighth Ōtani master closed the Sagimai Kiln that year, and because the glaze recipes had never been written down, the kasumi glaze was lost. The commercial kilns lost their protected local market as cheap porcelain from Arita and Seto arrived by steamship, and the number of kiln households in Suyama fell by about half between 1868 and 1880. From the 1880s Harukawa merchants turned to export. The Suyama Export Pottery Company (陶山輸出陶器会社), founded in 1886 by merchants of Gofukumachi, made Western forms such as tea sets, vases, jardinières and umbrella stands, decorated with kawasuji brushwork and impressed with the word HARUKAWA in Latin letters. The goods were shipped through Kobe to Britain, the United States and Australia. Exports peaked around 1907. After the First World War foreign demand collapsed, and the export company closed in 1923. On 15 July 1926 the Kagami Valley Railway, the forerunner of the Harukawa Railway, opened its first section, from Harukawa to Kamano, the station for Suyama, and carried clay and pottery as well as passengers. Kawabe Shūzan revival[edit] The revival of Harukawa ware as a craft is credited to Kawabe Shūzan (河辺秋山, 1881–1958), the son of a Suyama potter, who studied glaze chemistry in Kyoto before returning home. In 1919 he founded the Shūzan Kiln (秋山窯) in Suyama. He studied domain pieces lent by the Asagiri family, by then viscounts, and returned to Edo-period forms and to kawasuji brushwork, selling mainly to tea practitioners and to department stores in Osaka and Tokyo. He never managed to reproduce the kasumi glaze; his pale Shūzan blue ash glaze was an approximation. Shūzan took apprentices, and in 1938 accepted the 17-year-old Hanae Ishizuka, the first woman he trained. Suyama village was merged into Harukawa on 1 April 1942. In 1944–1945 the Suyama kilns were closed by wartime fuel rationing, but the district escaped the air raid of 29 July 1945, which burned 38 % of the city's urban area. After the war the Suyama Kiln Association organized the first Kamano Pottery Fair in 1952, the same year Ishizuka founded her own Kasumi Kiln. When Shūzan died in 1958, his son Kawabe Tōsai (河辺陶哉, 1912–1990) took over the Shūzan Kiln. Ishizuka and the kasumi glaze[edit] Main article: Hanae Ishizuka In 1958 the site of the Sagimai Kiln in the Ninomaru was excavated, revealing the kiln floor and about 6,800 shards. Hanae Ishizuka studied the shards for six years, comparing their glaze with ashes and minerals from the Suyama area. Her notebooks record 214 test firings. In 1964 she reproduced the domain kasumi glaze from rice-straw ash, wood ash and feldspar from the Kagami River. Her tea bowl Asamoya (1966) and the jar River Line (1967), which won a prize at the national traditional crafts exhibition, made the glaze widely known. Unlike the Ōtani family, Ishizuka taught the glaze openly. In 1970 she gave her base recipe to the Suyama Kiln Association, and by the late 1970s most Suyama kilns used a version of it, so that the kasumi glaze became the mark of Harukawa ware as a whole. She was designated a Living National Treasure in 1985. Designation in 1979[edit] On the strength of the revival, the national government designated Harukawa ware a Traditional Craft (伝統的工芸品) in 1979, under the 1974 law on the promotion of traditional craft industries. The designation requires Suyama clay, forming on the wheel or by hand, glazes based on natural ash, and decoration painted by hand; certified pieces carry the Traditional Craft label. The Center for Ceramic Studies of Harukawa University was set up in 1981 to work with the Suyama kilns, and in 1987 Harukawa became the sister city of Kellbridge, a pottery town in England. The industry since 1991[edit] Output grew from ¥1.9 billion in 1975 to ¥3.6 billion in 1985 and peaked at ¥4.6 billion in 1991, when 71 kilns were working. With the end of the bubble economy, demand for corporate gifts, wedding gifts and expensive tableware fell, and cheap imported tableware took much of the market. Production value fell to ¥3.4 billion in 2000, ¥2.4 billion in 2010 and a low of ¥1.6 billion in 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic emptied the shops of Suyama. It recovered to ¥2.1 billion in 2024, helped by record tourist numbers in Harukawa and by online sales through the Marketa marketplace. In 2024 the district had 38 kilns and about 210 workers; more than half of the kiln heads were over 60. The Suyama Kiln Association has run a two-year training course for new potters since 1996, and several younger potters have opened kilns since 2015. The industry is discussed further in Economy of Harukawa. Materials and techniques[edit] Clay[edit] Suyama clay is dug from beds of weathered granite and sedimentary clay in the hills around Suyama. It is rich in iron, with 4–6 % iron oxide, and fires to a dark gray-brown in reduction. Traditionally it was weathered outdoors for one to three years, then washed, sieved and wedged; most kilns now buy prepared clay from two clay works run by members of the Suyama Kiln Association. Kasumi glaze[edit] The kasumi glaze (霞釉, kasumi-yū, mist glaze ) is made from rice-straw ash, wood ash and feldspathic sand from the Kagami River. Ishizuka's base recipe of 1970 uses roughly four parts straw ash to three parts wood ash and three parts feldspar by weight. The silica of the straw ash gives the glaze its milky, opalescent look, and iron from the body gives it a faint blue-gray tone in reduction. Where the glaze runs thin over the rim, the iron of the clay shows through as a brown band, the iron-brown rim that is one of the ware's best-known features. Yuzu-hada[edit] Yuzu-hada (柚子肌, yuzu skin ) is a fine pitted texture in the glaze surface, like the peel of the yuzu citrus that is grown widely in Minori (see Yuzu cultivation in Minori). It comes from small bubbles that burst during firing and do not fully heal, and potters control it through the thickness of the glaze and the speed of cooling. On domain kiln pieces it was usually faint; modern potters often make it a feature. Kawasuji brushwork[edit] Kawasuji (川筋文, river line ) brushwork consists of loose, wavy parallel lines in iron oxide, painted quickly with a broad brush under the glaze. The lines are said to represent the currents of the Kagami River. The motif developed at the commercial kilns in the 18th century, was used heavily on export ware, and was taken up by Kawabe Shūzan and Hanae Ishizuka; her prize-winning jar of 1967 is named after it. Forming and firing[edit] Most pieces are thrown on the wheel; large storage jars are built up from coils and finished on a slow wheel. After a bisque firing at about 800 °C, pieces are glazed and fired in reduction at 1,250–1,280 °C. Historically all firing was done in wood-fired climbing kilns, and a firing of the Suyama Old Kiln took about three days. Most kilns now use gas kilns. About six kilns still fire with wood, and the Suyama Communal Kiln keeps a five-chamber wood-fired climbing kiln that is fired twice a year, in April before the Pottery Fair and in November. Forms[edit] The main traditional forms of Harukawa ware are: Tea bowls (chawan): the most prestigious form, made at the domain kiln from the 17th century; kasumi-glaze tea bowls with an iron-brown rim are the best-known pieces of the ware. Sake flasks (tokkuri): including the long-necked heron-neck flask (鷺首徳利, sagikubi-dokkuri), a Suyama form since the 18th century. Storage jars (tsubo and kame): made by the commercial kilns for water, miso, pickles and yuzu vinegar, up to about 90 cm tall, often with kawasuji brushwork. Plates: from small side dishes to large serving platters; Harukawa ware plates are widely used in local restaurants, including for the lantern buns of Harukawa cuisine. Incense burners (kōro): often in the shape of a stone lantern, made for temples and household altars. Since the 1960s the kilns have also made modern tableware such as coffee cups, bowls and vases, which make up most of today's production value. Organized by the Suyama Kiln Association since 1952, it draws about 150,000 visitors. About 120 stalls of kilns, dealers and students from Harukawa University line the 1.2 km street from Kamano Station to the Suyama Old Kiln, and many kilns open their workshops. Seconds are sold at a discount, and there are wheel-throwing demonstrations and a children's clay corner. Suyama is reached from Kamano Station on the Kagami Line, 13.5 km from Harukawa Central Station, where the Tsukikage limited express stops and many local trains turn back; the Harukawa Railway markets the district as the Kamano Pottery Village . City Bus 21 also runs hourly from Harukawa Central. The Kellbridge exchange potters usually show their work at the fair. Collections[edit] The Minori Prefectural Museum of Art in the castle's Sannomaru holds 1,240 pieces of Harukawa ware, the largest public collection, including 312 works and the glaze notebooks of Hanae Ishizuka, donated in 2010. The Harukawa Castle keep museum shows domain kiln pieces from the Asagiri collection, including the 1667 tea bowl. The Harukawa University Center for Ceramic Studies keeps the shards from the 1958 excavation of the Sagimai Kiln, deposited by the city, and a study collection of modern pieces. The Harukawa Ware Hall (春川焼会館), run by the Suyama Kiln Association near Kamano Station, has a permanent display, a shop and pottery workshops. The Kellbridge Pottery Museum in England holds about 140 pieces of export ware marked HARUKAWA . International links[edit] Harukawa has been the sister city of Kellbridge (ケルブリッジ), a pottery town in Staffordshire, United Kingdom, since 14 May 1987. The link grew out of the export trade: British collectors of export ware first visited Suyama in the early 1980s. Since 1988 the two towns have held an annual exchange of two young potters, who work for about three months in each other's studios. Mio Takano took part in 2015. Hanae Ishizuka presented a large kasumi-glaze jar to Kellbridge at the signing in 1987, and a joint exhibition marked the 30th anniversary of the link in 2017. It lies on the delta of the Kagami River, where the river flows into Minori Bay. As of 1 October 2025 the city had an estimated population of 412,800 in 191,300 households and an area of 486.3 km², giving a population density of about 849 people per km². It is by far the largest city in the prefecture, home to about 38% of its 1,086,400 people, and has been a core city since 1 April 1998. Harukawa grew up as the castle town of the Asagiri clan, who ruled the Harukawa Domain for eleven generations, from 1601 to 1871, from Harukawa Castle on Sagimai Hill, begun in 1603. It became the prefectural capital in 1871 and one of Japan's first cities under the municipal system on 1 April 1889. The city is known for Harukawa ware, a stoneware with a pale mist glaze made mainly in the Suyama district; for yuzu citrus (see Yuzu cultivation in Minori); for sea bream and oysters from the bay; and for the Harukawa Lantern Festival, held on the second weekend of October in memory of the victims of the Great Genbun Flood of 1739. Its economy rests on shipbuilding, machine tools, services and tourism, and it received a record 6.5 million tourist visitors in 2025. The privately owned Harukawa Railway, known as HaruTetsu, links Harukawa Central Station with the pottery district of Suyama, the hot-spring town of Tsukimi Onsen at the foot of Mount Tsukimi, and the ferry terminal at Minori Port. Before the castle was built, the fishing and market village at the mouth of the Kagami River was called Kagami-no-tsu (鏡津, harbor of the Kagami ). According to the clan genealogy Asagiri Kafu (朝霧家譜), compiled in the 1680s, Asagiri Tadamasa chose the new name in 1603, the year work on the castle began, recalling that he had first seen the river in the spring of 1601, swollen with snowmelt from Mount Tsukimi and lined with flowering trees. A second explanation, current in the Edo period, holds that the name expressed a wish that the new town would flourish like spring , a common motif in castle-town names of the early 17th century. The name passed from the castle town to the Harukawa Domain (春川藩), to the short-lived Harukawa Prefecture of 1871 and to the modern city. The older name survives in the river, in Kagami Shrine and in local institutions such as Kagami-no-tsu Elementary School in Uomachi. The castle's hill, Sagimai ( dancing heron ), gave its name to the castle's nickname, the main avenue, a bridge, the university's main campus and the city's football club. History[edit] Main article: History of Harukawa Before the castle town[edit] The oldest evidence of settlement is the Uchiura Shell Mound on the Uchiura Peninsula, a Jōmon-period midden from about 3000 BCE. From the 8th century the area belonged to Kagami District of Minori Province (実野国). From the 1400s until 1600 the district was ruled by the Uchiura clan (内浦氏) from Kurayama Castle (倉山城), a mountain fortress on Kurayama, the peak that now marks the city's northern boundary. Edo period[edit] After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, in which he fought on the Tokugawa side, Asagiri Tadamasa (1562–1629), head of a minor family of Kagami District, received the province of Minori with an assessed yield of 186,000 koku. He arrived in 1601, and in the spring of 1603 he broke ground for a new castle on Sagimai Hill beside the river. The castle town was laid out between 1603 and 1610, with samurai residences around the castle in present-day Shiromachi, a merchant quarter along Gofukumachi street and a fishermen's quarter at Uomachi. The keep was completed in 1611. In 1624 Tadamasa invited the potter Ōtani Sōemon from Hizen to found a domain kiln in the castle's Ninomaru, the origin of Harukawa ware. The second lord, Masatsugu, built the 3.2 km Masatsugu Embankment along the river between 1641 and 1648, and in 1651 the third lord, Tadakiyo, granted 10,000 koku to a branch family, the Uchiura Asagiri, leaving the main domain at 176,000 koku. After the Tenna famine of 1681–82 the fourth lord, Tadanobu, ordered in 1688 that every farming household plant three yuzu trees. On 4 October 1739, after three days of typhoon rain, the river overtopped the embankment in the Great Genbun Flood and killed about 1,140 people. In 1740 the sixth lord, Tadatoki, ordered lanterns to be floated on the river in memory of the dead, the origin of the Lantern Festival. On 15 June 1749 lightning set fire to the castle keep, which burned down; it was rebuilt to the same height between 1752 and 1755, and the Sagimai Gate followed in 1757. The eighth lord, Masahiro, founded the domain school Shūkōkan (修好館) in 1803. The Ansei earthquake of 1854 damaged the castle's north walls, which were repaired in 1856. Meiji period to 1945[edit] The domain sided with the new imperial government in the Boshin War of 1868. When the domains were abolished in 1871 it became Harukawa Prefecture, which was merged with two smaller prefectures on 14 November 1871 to form Minori Prefecture (then written 実野県), with Harukawa as its capital. In 1874 the castle buildings were sold off and the keep was demolished; only the Tatsumi Turret and the Sagimai Gate were kept. Oyster farming in the bay began in 1878, the newspaper Harukawa Nippō was founded in 1888, and Harukawa received city status on 1 April 1889 with about 31,200 inhabitants. Minori Bank was founded in 1897. The Kagami Valley Railway, founded in 1923, opened its first section, from Harukawa to Kamano, on 15 July 1926 under its chief engineer Kenzō Hattori; the line reached Tsukimi Onsen on 4 October 1931. The Harukawa Shipyard opened in 1937, and the pottery village of Suyama was merged into the city on 1 April 1942. On 29 July 1945 an air raid burned 38% of the urban area and killed 1,072 people. Since 1945[edit] Reconstruction was led by Tetsuo Saeki, deputy mayor from 1947 and mayor from 1951 to 1967, whose plan created the 50 m wide Sagimai Avenue (built 1949–1958). Harukawa University was founded on 31 May 1949. On 1 October 1954 the city absorbed the villages of Kawamata, Ichinose, Uchiura and Sakurahama. The Bayside Line opened to Minori Port on 1 October 1962. Between 1961 and 1966, 2.4 km² of the bay was reclaimed for the shipyard, and a reinforced-concrete reconstruction of the castle keep opened on 3 November 1966. In 1971 the prefecture's name was changed to the hiragana form みのり県, Minori Airport opened and the Ōkubo Dam was completed upstream. The Minori Prefectural Museum of Art opened in the castle grounds in 1983, the potter Hanae Ishizuka was designated a Living National Treasure in 1985, and the city signed a sister-city agreement with Kellbridge in the United Kingdom in 1987. Harukawa became a core city in 1998. A typhoon in September 2004 brought the worst flooding in seventy years, and the population peaked at 431,072 in the 2005 census. A new Harukawa Central Station building opened on 26 March 2011, and the castle keep reopened on 1 April 2023 after a seismic retrofit. Geography[edit] Harukawa occupies the delta and alluvial plain of the lower Kagami River and the hills around it, at the head of Minori Bay. The river, 94 km long, rises on the north slope of Mount Tsukimi (1,214 m), about 32 km north-east of the city center, and crosses the plain from north-east to south-west. Most of the city center lies at an elevation of about 4 m, and parts of Uomachi and Shiomi stand on land reclaimed from the bay. Harukawa Castle stands on Sagimai Hill (鷺舞山, 48 m), an isolated hill on the left (east) bank of the river 2.6 km from its mouth. North of the plain the land rises to forested hills; the highest point in the city is Kurayama (倉山, 683 m) on the northern boundary, site of the medieval castle. To the south the hilly Uchiura Peninsula, whose terraced slopes are planted with yuzu, forms the south side of the inner bay, with the beach of Sakurahama on its shore. Harukawa borders the city of Kitano to the north, the town of Kagami to the north-east, the city of Takasu to the east and the city of Nishiura to the south-west. Districts[edit] The city has no wards. Its best-known districts are: Main districts of Harukawa District Japanese Description Shiromachi 城町 Castle and civic center: Castle Park, City Hall, the prefectural government, the Museum of Art and the head office of Minori Bank Ekimae 駅前 The area around Harukawa Central Station and its station building, Harukawa Central Terrace (2011) Gofukumachi 呉服町 Old merchant street with a covered shopping arcade; the Hundred Lantern Road during the festival Uomachi 魚町 Fishing port and central fish market (1956); birthplace of Michiyo Tōno and Kenzō Hattori Shiomi 汐見 Riverside district by Shiomi Bridge, where the festival's floating lanterns are collected; nearest station Ichiba Suyama 陶山 Pottery district north-east of the center, reached from Kamano Station (13.5 km); 38 kilns, the Suyama Old Kiln and the Kamano Pottery Fair Uchiura 内浦 Former village (merged 1954) on the Uchiura Peninsula; shell mound and yuzu terraces Sakurahama 桜浜 Former village (merged 1954) with the city's main beach, near Minori Port Climate[edit] Main article: Climate of Harukawa Harukawa has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cfa) with hot, humid summers and mild winters. On the 1991–2020 normals of the Harukawa Local Meteorological Observatory, the annual mean temperature is 16.5 °C and annual precipitation is 1,878.2 mm, falling on 110.7 days; the city receives 2,082.9 hours of sunshine a year. August is the hottest month (mean 28.1 °C, mean high 32.3 °C) and also the sunniest (216.0 hours); January is the coldest (mean 5.6 °C). June, at the height of the tsuyu rainy season, is the wettest month with 312.5 mm, ahead of September (289.7 mm), when typhoons approach; January is the driest (52.4 mm), so June brings about six times as much rain as January. The rainy season usually lasts from about 6 June to 19 July, and about 2.6 typhoons approach the city each year. Snow falls on about two days a year and seldom settles. The highest temperature on record is 38.4 °C (7 August 2018) and the lowest −6.2 °C (28 January 1981). The heaviest daily rainfall, 287.0 mm on 19 September 2004, caused the city's worst flood since 1934. Inland it is markedly cooler: Tsukimi Onsen, at 310 m, has an annual mean of 13.8 °C, and the summit of Mount Tsukimi is about 7.5 °C colder than the city. Demographics[edit] On 1 October 2025 Harukawa had an estimated 412,800 inhabitants in 191,300 households. The 2020 census counted 418,316 people. The population grew from about 31,200 when city status was granted in 1889 to 96,412 at the first national census in 1920 and 152,884 in 1940. The air raid and wartime evacuation reduced it to 149,310 by 1947. The merger with four villages on 1 October 1954 raised it from 171,346 in 1950 to 238,517 in 1955, an increase of 39% in five years. Growth continued with the shipyard and new housing estates along the Kagami Line, and the population passed 400,000 in the late 1980s (409,788 in 1990), peaking at 431,072 in the 2005 census. Since then it has fallen slowly, by about 3% between 2005 and 2020, because deaths now exceed births; net migration has been close to zero since the mid-2010s. In 2025, 30.4% of residents were aged 65 or over. Foreign residents numbered 6,920 (1.7%), the largest groups coming from Vietnam, China and the Philippines, many of them working at the shipyard and in food processing. The mayor, Takuya Hirose (広瀬拓也), an independent who worked in the city government for 28 years and a 1986 graduate of the Faculty of Economics of Harukawa University, was first elected in November 2018 and re-elected in November 2022. He is seeking a third term at the mayoral election of 8 November 2026, against the former prefectural assembly member Michiko Sawada; flood control is the main issue. The city assembly has 44 members elected for four-year terms; the next assembly election is due in April 2027. City Hall stands in Shiromachi, facing Castle Park. As a core city since 1 April 1998, Harukawa exercises some powers normally held by the prefecture, such as running its own public health center and licensing restaurants and care homes. Its general-account budget for FY2026 is ¥187.2 billion. Harukawa is also the seat of the Minori Prefectural Government, headed since 2017 by Governor Hiroshi Takemura, and of the Minori Prefectural Assembly. Among the city's former mayors, Tetsuo Saeki (1951–1967) is remembered for postwar reconstruction, the 1954 merger and the rebuilding of the castle keep. Economy[edit] Main article: Economy of Harukawa Harukawa's gross city product was ¥1.68 trillion in FY2022, about ¥4.0 million per resident. Manufacturing is the largest sector (21.4%), followed by wholesale and retail (13.8%), health and social care (12.6%) and real estate (11.2%). The largest industrial employers are the Harukawa Shipyard of Minori Heavy Industries, opened in 1937 and now on land reclaimed from the bay, with about 3,100 workers, and Kagami Precision (鏡精機), a machine-tool maker founded in 1952, with about 2,400. Harukawa University and its hospital employ about 4,200 people, Minori Bank (founded 1897, head office in Shiromachi) about 1,850 and the Harukawa Railway 684. Unemployment was 2.4% in 2025. Traditional industries remain visible. In 2024 the 38 kilns of the Harukawa ware industry employed about 210 people and produced ware worth ¥2.1 billion, less than half of the 1991 peak of ¥4.6 billion from 71 kilns. The Uomachi central fish market, opened in 1956, handles sea bream, oysters and other catches from Minori Bay, and the terraces of the Uchiura Peninsula are among the prefecture's main yuzu-growing areas. Tourism has grown in importance. The city received a record 6.5 million tourist visitors in 2025, up from 6.2 million in 2024 and 2.9 million in 2020, with 1.94 million overnight stays. The castle keep (512,000 visitors in FY2024), the Minori Bay Aquarium (466,000), the Lantern Festival (380,000 in 2025) and the Museum of Art (186,000) are the leading attractions. The main shopping areas are the covered arcade of Gofukumachi and Harukawa Central Terrace, the station building opened in 2011; the Kumo Mobile Harukawa Central shop is a minute's walk from the station's South Exit. Transport[edit] Rail[edit] See also: Harukawa Railway, Kagami Line, Bayside Line Rail services are run by the Harukawa Railway (HaruTetsu), a private company founded in 1923 as the Kagami Valley Railway, with its head office in Ekimae. Both of its lines start at Harukawa Central Station, which had 38,420 boardings a day in FY2025. The Kagami Line runs 38.6 km up the Kagami River valley to Tsukimi Onsen, with 14 stations, seven of them in Harukawa: Harukawa Central, Shiromachi, Harukawa Daigaku-mae, Kawabata, Yanagihara, Nishi-Haruno and Kamano. Local trains stop at every station and take 63 minutes end to end; on weekday daytimes they run every 30 minutes as far as Kamano and hourly beyond, and hourly rapid trains take 55 minutes. The limited express Tsukikage, which stops at Shiromachi, Kamano and Kagami-kyō, covers the line in 39 minutes. The Bayside Line runs 16.2 km along the north shore of the bay to Minori Port, with nine stations, all in the city; its trains stop at every station, run every 15 minutes in the weekday peaks and every 20 minutes on weekday middays and at weekends, and take 28 minutes. HaruTetsu carried about 41 million passengers in FY2025, with 112,430 boardings a day at its 22 stations. Fares start at ¥170; Harukawa Central to Tsukimi Onsen costs ¥730, plus a ¥760 surcharge on the Tsukikage, and to Minori Port ¥410. The HaruCa contactless card, introduced in 2012, is accepted on trains, Harukawa City Bus and Tsukimi Bus, and fares paid with it are up to ¥18 cheaper. The timetable revision of Saturday 14 November 2026 adds a Tsukikage stop at Tsukimi-guchi, which lengthens the journey to 41 minutes, and gives the Bayside Line a train every 15 minutes on weekday middays as well. Shiromachi Station, 1.8 km from Harukawa Central, is the nearest to the castle, eight minutes' walk from its Castle Exit. Roads and buses[edit] The North Exit of Harukawa Central has a bus terminal with 16 bays for Harukawa City Bus, whose route 1, the Castle Loop, runs every 12 minutes and reaches the castle in 6 minutes; long-distance highway coaches stop at the South Exit. Sagimai Avenue, 50 m wide, is the main axis of the rebuilt city center, and the Minori Expressway serves the city through the Harukawa interchange. In the city center three road bridges cross the Kagami River: Sagimai Bridge, Kagami Bridge (386 m, opened 1932) and Shiomi Bridge. Air and sea[edit] Minori Airport, 22 km south-west of the center in Nishiura, opened in 1971 and handles domestic flights; airport limousine buses leave the South Exit of Harukawa Central every 30 minutes, take 55 minutes and cost ¥1,300. Ferries from Minori Port reach Kasumi Island in the bay in 35 minutes. Culture[edit] Festivals[edit] Main article: Harukawa Lantern Festival The Harukawa Lantern Festival (春川灯籠まつり) is the city's largest event, held on the second weekend of October (10–11 October in 2026). It began in 1740 as a memorial for the victims of the 1739 flood, and its organizers count the 2026 festival as the 282nd. On the Saturday evening (18:00–20:30) about 12,000 floating lanterns of Tsukimi washi are released below Kagami Bridge and drift 1.4 km to Shiomi Bridge, where nets collect them. On the Sunday about 3,500 lanterns painted by citizens and schoolchildren hang over Gofukumachi street as the Hundred Lantern Road , 36 large lantern floats parade from Kagami Shrine to the castle, and 4,000 fireworks are launched over the bay at 19:30. Attendance was 380,000 in 2025; the record is 405,000 (2019). The Kamano Pottery Fair (釜野陶器市) has been held every year since 1952 on the first weekend of May, in front of Kamano Station and in the Suyama pottery district, and draws about 150,000 visitors to the stalls of the kilns. In spring about 1,100 cherry trees bloom in Castle Park, and the park's 600 maples turn in November. Harukawa ware[edit] Main article: Harukawa ware Harukawa ware (春川焼) is a stoneware made since 1624, when Asagiri Tadamasa invited the potter Ōtani Sōemon from Hizen to found the domain kiln. It is known for the kasumi ( mist ) glaze, a milky pale blue-grey glaze, and for kawasuji brushwork of loose wavy lines in iron oxide. The commercial kilns of Suyama date from the 1680s; the 14-chamber Suyama Old Kiln, used from about 1690 to 1931, has been a National Historic Site since 4 October 2015. After a long decline the ware was revived from 1919 by the potter Kawabe Shūzan, and his pupil Hanae Ishizuka recreated the domain's kasumi glaze in 1964. Harukawa ware was designated a Traditional Craft by the national government in 1979. Cuisine[edit] Main article: Cuisine of Harukawa The city's signature dish is tai-yuzu meshi (鯛柚子めし), sea bream from Minori Bay cooked on rice in a clay pot with yuzu peel, at its best from March to May. Other local dishes include kagami-jiru, a clear soup of grilled ayu from the Kagami River (June–October); Minori kaki-nabe, an oyster hot pot with white miso and yuzu (November–March); sagimai-zushi, pressed sushi of Spanish mackerel; and yuzu-miso oden sold at street stalls in Uomachi. Tōrō manjū, lantern-shaped buns with white bean paste, were created in 1911 by the Gofukumachi confectioner Kikuya. Harukawa households spent ¥4,812 on sea bream in 2024, the most of any prefectural capital. Shrines and temples[edit] Kagami Shrine (鏡神社) enshrines a bronze mirror that, according to legend, a princess lost in the river and a fisherman later recovered; its autumn festival falls on the Sunday of the Lantern Festival. Kōun-ji (光雲寺) is the family temple of the Asagiri clan and holds the graves of several of its lords. Museums[edit] The Minori Prefectural Museum of Art, opened in 1983 in the castle's Sannomaru, holds about 9,600 works, including 1,240 pieces of Harukawa ware. The museum in the castle keep displays the armor and documents of the Asagiri clan, including the 2,300 Asagiri family papers donated in 1966, and has an observation floor on its sixth floor. The Old Main Building of Harukawa University (1931) houses the university museum, and the Minori Bay Aquarium, opened in 1997, stands by Minori-kōen Station on the Bayside Line. Literature and media[edit] The novelist Michiyo Tōno, born in Uomachi, set her best-known novel, The River Mirror (1956), in the city at the time of the 1739 flood; the city has awarded the Michiyo Tōno Literary Prize since 1989. The local daily Harukawa Nippō (春川日報) was founded in 1888, and its English edition, The Harukawa Herald, has appeared since 1998. Sport[edit] Harukawa Sagimai FC plays in the third tier of Japanese football. The Harukawa Castle Marathon, run each February from Castle Park along the river, was first held in 2012. Education[edit] Harukawa University, a national university, was founded on 31 May 1949 by merging the Minori Higher Commercial School (1923), the Minori Normal School (1874) and Harukawa Medical College (1943). It has seven faculties, 8,940 undergraduates and 1,620 graduate students (May 2025), and three main sites: the Sagimai Campus (Harukawa Daigaku-mae Station), the adjacent Medical Campus with the medical faculty and a 720-bed hospital, and the Yuzuhara Field Station in the town of Kagami. The city also has Minori Prefectural University (1992) and the private Harukawa Gakuin University (1951). The city runs 58 elementary schools and 27 junior high schools. The prefectural Shūkōkan High School takes its name from the domain school founded in 1803. International relations[edit] Harukawa has been the sister city of Kellbridge (ケルブリッジ), a pottery town in Staffordshire, United Kingdom, since 14 May 1987. The link grew out of contacts between the potters of the two towns, and since 1988 each town has sent two young potters to work in the other every year. A joint exhibition marked the 30th anniversary of the link in 2017. Notable people[edit] Asagiri Tadamasa (1562–1629), first lord of the Harukawa Domain and founder of the castle and town Kawabe Shūzan (1881–1958), potter who revived Harukawa ware from 1919 Kenzō Hattori (1873–1941), railway engineer who built the Kagami Line, born in Uomachi Tetsuo Saeki (1902–1979), mayor from 1951 to 1967, born in Kawamata village Michiyo Tōno (1914–1987), novelist, born in Uomachi Hanae Ishizuka (1921–2009), potter and Living National Treasure, born in Suyama Ren Mizuhara (born 1956), potter, head of the Kasumi Kiln since 2009 See also[edit] History of Harukawa Economy of Harukawa Climate of Harukawa Harukawa Castle Harukawa Lantern Festival Minori Prefecture Minori Bay Notes[edit] ^ Some sources give 1612 for the completion of the keep, because the gilded shachihoko roof ornaments and the final fittings were installed in the spring of that year. ^ The length of 94 km is the figure of the national river authority. The prefecture's own river register gives 96 km because it also counts the Hosoya headwater stream. ^ On the older 1961–1990 normals September (about 301 mm) was wetter than June (about 287 mm), and older guidebooks still name September as the wettest month. ^ The figure of 412,800 is the prefecture's estimate, which starts from the 2020 census and adds births, deaths and moves recorded since. x: History of Harukawa春川市の歴史 The Tatsumi Turret of Harukawa Castle (1609), the oldest surviving building of the castle town Location of Harukawa in Minori Prefecture Key dates Earliest settlement c. 3000 BCE (Uchiura Shell Mound) Former name Kagami-no-tsu (before 1603) Castle town founded 1603 Domain Harukawa Domain, 1601–1871 (Asagiri clan) Prefectural capital 1871 (Minori Prefecture) City status 1 April 1889 Major merger 1 October 1954 (four villages) Core city 1 April 1998 Population 1889 31,200 Peak (2005 census) 431,072 2025 (estimate) 412,800 The history of Harukawa covers the human settlement of the lower Kagami River and the shores of Minori Bay from the Jōmon period to the present city of Harukawa, the capital of Minori Prefecture. A fishing and harbor village called Kagami-no-tsu for most of its early history, the place became a castle town in 1603, when Asagiri Tadamasa began Harukawa Castle and gave the town its present name. It was ruled by the Asagiri clan for 270 years, became the prefectural capital in 1871 and a city on 1 April 1889, and grew in the 20th century around its port, its shipyard and the Harukawa Railway. Much of the center was destroyed in the air raid of 29 July 1945. Under Mayor Tetsuo Saeki (1951–1967) the city was rebuilt, merged with four villages and reached its present size; its population peaked at 431,072 in 2005 and stood at an estimated 412,800 in 2025. Excavations in 1934 and 1972 recovered oyster and clam shells, bone fishhooks, Jōmon pottery and the remains of pit dwellings, showing that the bay shore was settled by fishing communities more than 5,000 years ago. Remains of the Yayoi period, including rice paddies, have been found on the higher parts of the Kagami delta. In the 8th century the area belonged to Kagami District (鏡郡) of Minori Province (実野国) under the ritsuryō system. The provincial capital lay inland, and the river mouth served as a small harbor known as Kagami-no-tsu (鏡津), the harbor of the Kagami . The river's name, meaning mirror , is explained by its clear, still pools and by the legend of a bronze mirror lost by a princess and recovered by a fisherman; the mirror is said to be the sacred object of Kagami Shrine, which local tradition dates to the 9th century. Sengoku period[edit] From the 1400s until 1600 the region was ruled by the Uchiura clan (内浦氏), a local warrior family that took its name from the Uchiura Peninsula. Its seat was Kurayama Castle (倉山城), a mountain castle on Kurayama (683 m), which is now the highest point of the city on its northern boundary. The Uchiura controlled Kagami-no-tsu and the river trade, fought repeatedly with neighbors in the 16th century and, at the decisive battle of Sekigahara in 1600, took the side of the Western Army. After the Tokugawa victory they lost their lands. Edo period[edit] The Asagiri and the castle town[edit] Asagiri Tadamasa (1562–1629), the son of a minor family of Kagami District who had fought on the Tokugawa side at Sekigahara, received Minori with an assessed yield of 186,000 koku and arrived in 1601. He first lived in Kurayama Castle, but in 1603 began a new castle on a low hill beside Kagami-no-tsu. Ground was broken in the third month of Keichō 8 (spring 1603); the hill was named Sagimai, Heron Dance , after herons that were said to have circled over it that day, and Tadamasa renamed the settlement Harukawa, spring river , recalling, according to the clan genealogy, the river in spring flood as he had first seen it in 1601. The keep was completed in 1611. Kurayama Castle was abandoned in 1615 under the shogunate's one-castle-per-province law. The castle town was laid out between 1603 and 1610. Samurai lived in Shiromachi, around the castle; merchants in Gofukumachi ( draper's town ), the main commercial street south of the castle; and fishermen and fish dealers in Uomachi near the river mouth. Potters later settled in Suyama, north-east of the town, where the clay was good. A domain census of 1721 counted 21,400 townspeople, not including samurai households. Embankment, pottery and yuzu[edit] The domain's greatest public work was the Masatsugu Embankment (正次堤), a 3.2 km levee along the river above the town, built from 1641 to 1648 under the 2nd lord, Asagiri Masatsugu. In 1624 Tadamasa had invited the potter Ōtani Sōemon from Hizen to set up a domain kiln in the castle's Ninomaru, the beginning of Harukawa ware; commercial kilns followed in Suyama from the 1680s. In 1651 the 3rd lord, Tadakiyo, gave 10,000 koku to a branch family, the Uchiura Asagiri, reducing the main domain to 176,000 koku. The Tenna famine of 1681–82 hit the domain hard. In response the 4th lord, Asagiri Tadanobu, ordered in 1688 that every farming household plant three yuzu trees, which could grow on slopes unfit for rice. The order laid the foundation of yuzu cultivation in Minori, today the third-largest in Japan, and of the yuzu flavors of the local cuisine. The Great Genbun Flood and the lantern memorial[edit] On 4 October 1739 (Genbun 4), after three days of typhoon rain, the Kagami River overtopped the Masatsugu Embankment and flooded the lower castle town. The Great Genbun Flood killed about 1,140 people, most of them in the fishing quarter of Uomachi and the low ground of Shiomi, and destroyed much of the rice harvest. The 5th lord, Masayoshi, died the following year. In 1740 his successor, Asagiri Tadatoki, ordered a memorial service in which lanterns were floated on the river for the dead. The memorial was repeated every year on the anniversary of the flood and grew into the Harukawa Lantern Festival. After the flood the Masatsugu Embankment was raised and lengthened. The disaster and the first memorial are the subject of Michiyo Tōno's novel The River Mirror (1956). Fire, reform and the end of the domain[edit] On 15 June 1749 lightning struck the castle keep, which burned down. Tadatoki rebuilt it between 1752 and 1755, partly with a levy on the merchants of Gofukumachi, and the Sagimai Gate was rebuilt in 1757. The cost burdened the domain for decades. The 8th lord, Asagiri Masahiro, founded the domain school, the Shūkōkan (修好館), in 1803. It taught Confucian classics, medicine and, from the 1840s, Western gunnery. The Ansei earthquake of December 1854 damaged the castle's north walls and houses in the town; the walls were repaired in 1856. A cholera epidemic forced the cancellation of the lantern memorial in 1863. In the Boshin War of 1868 the domain, under its 11th and last lord Asagiri Tadanori, sided with the new Meiji government. Meiji period to 1945[edit] Prefectural capital and city[edit] The domains were abolished in 1871. Harukawa Domain became Harukawa Prefecture in the summer, and on 14 November 1871 it was merged with two smaller prefectures, including Uchiura Prefecture, the former branch domain, to form Minori Prefecture (実野県), with Harukawa as its capital. In 1874 the castle buildings were sold and the keep was demolished; only the Tatsumi Turret and the Sagimai Gate were kept. The same year Minori Normal School was founded. Oyster farming began in Minori Bay in 1878, and the newspaper Harukawa Nippō was founded in 1888. On 1 April 1889, when the municipal system came into force, Harukawa became one of Japan's first cities, with 31,200 inhabitants. Minori Bank was founded in 1897. In 1910 the Lantern Festival was fixed to October in the solar calendar, and in 1911 the confectioner Kikuya of Gofukumachi created the lantern-shaped tōrō manjū. The potter Kawabe Shūzan began the revival of Harukawa ware in 1919. The Kagami Valley Railway (鏡谷鉄道) was founded in 1923 and, under its chief engineer Kenzō Hattori, opened the first section of the Kagami Line, from Harukawa to Kamano, on 15 July 1926. The line reached Tsukimi Onsen on 4 October 1931, opening the hot springs of Tsukimi Onsen to visitors from the city. Minori Higher Commercial School was founded in 1923 and moved into its red-brick main building in 1931. The Kagami Bridge opened on 20 March 1932. A flood in 1934 again inundated the lower town. Industry and war[edit] The Harukawa Shipyard opened on the bay in 1937. With the shipyard and the war economy the population passed 150,000 by 1940. Suyama village was merged into the city on 1 April 1942, and Harukawa Medical College was founded in 1943. The Lantern Festival was suspended from 1944. On the night of 29 July 1945, an air raid burned 38 % of the urban area and killed 1,072 people. Uomachi, the station area and much of Gofukumachi were destroyed, as were buildings in the Sannomaru of the castle; the Tatsumi Turret, the Sagimai Gate and the Kagami Bridge survived. At the census of 1947 the city had 149,310 inhabitants, fewer than in 1940. Postwar period[edit] Reconstruction[edit] The Lantern Festival was revived in October 1947 at the initiative of the deputy mayor, Tetsuo Saeki, a former prefectural civil engineer, and was seen as a memorial for the dead of 1945 as well as of 1739. Saeki also drew up the reconstruction plan, whose centerpiece was the 50 m wide Sagimai Avenue (鷺舞通り), built between 1949 and 1958 from the station square past the castle and designed as a firebreak as well as a main street. Harukawa University was founded on 31 May 1949 by merging the Higher Commercial School, the Normal School and the Medical College. Saeki was elected mayor in April 1951 and served four terms, to 1967. The university opened its Sagimai Campus in 1951, the year the Kagami Valley Railway took its present name, Harukawa Railway; the Kagami Line was electrified in 1952 and the first Kamano Pottery Fair was held the same year. On 1 October 1954 the city merged with the four villages of Kawamata, Ichinose, Uchiura and Sakurahama, which raised its population from 171,346 (1950) to 238,517 (1955). The Uomachi central fish market opened in 1956, and the Tsukimi–Kagami Prefectural Natural Park was designated in 1959. Reclamation and the keep[edit] The Bayside Line opened along the bay to Minori Port on 1 October 1962, for passengers and freight, and Harukawa Station was renamed Harukawa Central the same day. Between 1961 and 1966 the city and the prefecture reclaimed 2.4 km² of Minori Bay for the expansion of the shipyard. The oyster fishermen of the bay opposed the project; their 1965 lawsuit was settled in 1968 with compensation of ¥380 million. The castle keep, rebuilt in reinforced concrete with the help of a citizens' donation campaign, opened on 3 November 1966, and the Asagiri family gave about 2,300 documents to its museum. 1970s and 1980s[edit] 1971, the centenary of the prefecture, brought three changes: the prefecture's name was changed on 1 April to the hiragana form みのり県, because the characters 実野 were often misread; Minori Airport opened 22 km south-west of the city; and the Ōkubo Dam on the upper Kagami River was completed. Harukawa ware was designated a Traditional Craft by the national government in 1979, the Minori Prefectural Museum of Art opened in the castle's Sannomaru in 1983, and the potter Hanae Ishizuka was named a Living National Treasure in 1985. On 14 May 1987 Harukawa became a sister city of Kellbridge, a pottery town in Staffordshire, England, and the same year the limited express Tsukikage began running to Tsukimi Onsen. The eight-volume Harukawa City History was completed in 1989, the year the city founded the Michiyo Tōno Literary Prize. Since 1990[edit] Harukawa ware production peaked in 1991 at ¥4.6 billion from 71 kilns. Minori Prefectural University opened in 1992, and the Minori Bay Aquarium in 1997. On 1 April 1998 Harukawa became a core city, gaining powers normally held by the prefecture; the same year the Harukawa Nippō launched its English edition, The Harukawa Herald, and the Bayside Line was elevated between Harukawa Central and Shinkō-dōri. Since 2000 the Lantern Festival has been held on the second weekend of October. A typhoon in September 2004 brought a record daily rainfall of 287.0 mm on 19 September and flooded low-lying districts along the river. The 2005 census recorded the city's highest population, 431,072; it has declined at every census since, to 418,316 in 2020, as the population ages (30.4 % were 65 or older in 2025). The new Harukawa Central Station building opened on 26 March 2011, and the HaruCa IC card was introduced in 2012. The Suyama Old Kiln was designated a National Historic Site on 4 October 2015. Takuya Hirose, a city official for 28 years, was elected mayor as an independent in November 2018 and re-elected in 2022; he is seeking a third term at the election of 8 November 2026. The castle keep closed for a seismic retrofit in 2019, and the 8000 series trains entered service on the Tsukikage the same year. The COVID-19 pandemic cut tourist visitors from 6.1 million in 2019 to 2.9 million in 2020, when the Lantern Festival was cancelled for the first time since the war. The keep reopened on 1 April 2023, and visitors reached a record 6.5 million in 2025. The prefecture estimated the population at 412,800 on 1 October 2025. The 2026 Lantern Festival, on 10–11 October, is counted as the 282nd by the festival committee. Population[edit] The population grew from 31,200 in 1889 to more than 150,000 by 1940, fell during the war, and rose sharply after the 1954 merger and with postwar industrial growth. Growth slowed in the 1990s, and the city has been losing population since the 2005 peak. It is a nine-span reinforced concrete arch bridge, 386 m long, and links the Gofukumachi district on the east bank with the districts on the west bank. Of the three bridges in the city center it is the middle one, between the Sagimai Bridge upstream and the Shiomi Bridge downstream. The bridge opened on 20 March 1932, replacing a wooden bridge of 1879. It survived the air raid of 29 July 1945 with minor damage and was widened from 14 m to 22 m in 1978, when the roadway was given four lanes. During the Harukawa Lantern Festival on the second weekend of October, about 12,000 floating lanterns are released on the Saturday evening just downstream of the bridge and drift 1.4 km to the Shiomi Bridge, where nets collect them. The bridge, with the keep of Harukawa Castle behind it, is one of the most photographed views of the city. It runs from Harukawa Central Station in Harukawa up the valley of the Kagami River to the hot-spring town of Tsukimi Onsen, serving 14 stations in the city of Harukawa and the towns of Kagami and Tsukimi. It is double track for its first 13.5 km to Kamano and single track beyond. The line was planned by the engineer Kenzō Hattori for the Kagami Valley Railway, as HaruTetsu was called until 1951, and opened in four stages between 1926 and 1931; it was built to 1,067 mm gauge and electrified in 1952. Local trains take 63 minutes from end to end and rapid trains 55 minutes, and the limited express Tsukikage covers the line in 39 minutes. In FY2025 its stations other than Harukawa Central had 43,590 boardings a day, against 30,420 at those of the Bayside Line. Harukawa Central to Kamano[edit] Leaving the elevated platforms of Harukawa Central, the line heads north-east through the city. Shiromachi (1.8 km) is the nearest station to Harukawa Castle: from its Castle Exit on the west side the keep is about eight minutes' walk uphill, and its River Exit on the east side leads to the Kagami River and a gallery street of Harukawa ware shops. Harukawa Daigaku-mae (3.6 km), opened in 1951, serves the Sagimai Campus of Harukawa University, whose main gate is three minutes from the station, and the neighboring Medical Campus with the University Hospital, seven minutes on foot. Kawabata (5.9 km) was added in 1968 for a new housing estate. Beyond Yanagihara (8.2 km) the line follows the left (east) bank of the river past rice fields and orchards to Nishi-Haruno (10.7 km), between Kawamata and Ichinose, two former villages merged into Harukawa in 1954. Kamano (13.5 km) is the station for the Suyama pottery district, where Harukawa ware is made and where the Kamano Pottery Fair is held every year on the first weekend of May in front of the station; the railway markets the district as the Kamano Pottery Village , which is also served by City Bus 21 from Harukawa Central once an hour. The double track ends here, many local trains turn back, and the company's depot, Kamano Depot, lies just beyond the station. Kamano to Kagami-kyō[edit] Beyond Kamano the single track enters the town of Kagami at the unstaffed Ōtsuka (16.4 km) and reaches Yuzuhara (19.8 km), surrounded by the terraced orchards that grow much of the prefecture's yuzu and home to Harukawa University's Yuzuhara Field Station. Upstream of Yuzuhara the line passes the Ōkubo Dam, and at Futamata, where the Hosoya River joins the Kagami just below Kagami-kyō Station, it crosses to the right bank on the Futamata Bridge. Kagami-kyō to Tsukimi Onsen[edit] Kagami-kyō (23.6 km) stands at the mouth of the Kagami Gorge and is the start of the five-hour west trail up Mount Tsukimi. After the unstaffed Nakazawa (27.1 km), the last station in Kagami, the line reaches Hotarudani (30.4 km), the first station in the town of Tsukimi, known for its fireflies in June; with 190 boardings a day it is the quietest on the line. From here the line climbs at up to 25 ‰ into the 2,184 m Tsukimi Tunnel, which takes it under a spur of Mount Tsukimi to Tsukimi-guchi (34.9 km), where a statue of Hattori stands in front of the station. The last 3.7 km run up the Tsukimi Valley to the terminus at Tsukimi Onsen (38.6 km), from where Tsukimi Bus route 5 takes 25 minutes to the Tsukimi Ropeway. History[edit] Main article: Harukawa Railway Hattori became chief engineer of the newly founded Kagami Valley Railway in 1923 and chose a route that kept close to the river, avoiding the hills on either side. The line was built to 1,067 mm gauge from the start and worked by steam. It opened in four stages: Opening of the Kagami Line Date Section Length Notes 15 July 1926 Harukawa – Kamano 13.5 km Steam; Shiromachi, Yanagihara and Nishi-Haruno opened at the same time 20 May 1928 Kamano – Yuzuhara 6.3 km Ōtsuka 3 November 1929 Yuzuhara – Hotarudani 10.6 km Futamata Bridge; Kagami-kyō and Nakazawa stations 4 October 1931 Hotarudani – Tsukimi Onsen 8.2 km Tsukimi Tunnel; Tsukimi-guchi station Harukawa Daigaku-mae station opened on 1 April 1951, the year the company was renamed the Harukawa Railway, and the line was electrified at 1,500 V DC in 1952. On 1 October 1968 the double track was completed as far as Kamano and Kawabata station opened. In 1994 track improvements raised the maximum speed from 85 km/h to the present 95 km/h. The flood of September 2004 washed away part of the embankment near Ichinose, and trains between Yanagihara and Yuzuhara were replaced by buses for 23 days. When Harukawa Central was rebuilt as an elevated station in 2011, the first 1.9 km of the line were raised onto a viaduct. Services[edit] Local and rapid trains[edit] Local trains, formed of two-car 2000 series sets, call at every station and take 63 minutes from end to end. On weekdays during the day they run every 30 minutes between Harukawa Central and Kamano, where every other train turns back, and hourly beyond Kamano; in the morning and evening peaks through trains to Tsukimi Onsen run every 30 minutes. Beyond Kamano trains are driver-only, and passengers boarding at the unstaffed stations (Ōtsuka, Nakazawa and Hotarudani) touch HaruCa on the platform reader or take a boarding certificate from a machine on the platform. Rapid trains (快速, kaisoku) run hourly between Harukawa Central and Tsukimi Onsen and take 55 minutes. They stop at every station except Kawabata, Nishi-Haruno and Ōtsuka. Tsukikage[edit] The limited express Tsukikage runs 7 trains to Tsukimi Onsen and 8 back on weekdays, and 9 and 10 on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. It stops at Shiromachi, Kamano and Kagami-kyō and takes 39 minutes from Harukawa Central to Tsukimi Onsen. All seats are reserved; for the whole line the limited express surcharge is ¥760 on top of the ordinary fare of ¥730, or ¥1,490 in all. On the evenings of the Harukawa Lantern Festival (10–11 October 2026) extra local trains run between Harukawa Central and Kamano or Kagami-kyō, and Tsukikage 21, 24, 25 and 28 do not stop at Shiromachi. Timetable revision of November 2026[edit] On Saturday 14 November 2026 HaruTetsu will revise the timetable. Every Tsukikage will also stop at Tsukimi-guchi, which lengthens the journey to 41 minutes; Tsukikage 1 on weekdays will leave Harukawa Central at 7:25 and reach Tsukimi Onsen at 8:06, instead of 7:30 and 8:09. Rapid trains will also call at Kawabata, taking one minute longer. Last trains will run later: on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays the last train from Tsukimi Onsen will leave at 21:40 (Harukawa Central 22:43) instead of 21:05, and the last weekday northbound train from Harukawa Central, at 23:20, will run to Kagami-kyō (arriving 23:59) instead of Kamano. On the Bayside Line, weekday trains between 10:00 and 16:40 will run every 15 minutes instead of every 20. Fares, surcharges and pass prices do not change, and the new station timetables are published on 1 November. Infrastructure[edit] The Futamata Bridge (二股橋梁), completed in 1929 to Hattori's design, carries the line over the Kagami River just above its confluence with the Hosoya River, a short distance below Kagami-kyō Station. It is 218 m long, with three steel truss spans on masonry piers and short plate-girder approaches, and is the longest bridge on the HaruTetsu network. It was strengthened for electrification in 1952 and was selected as civil engineering heritage by the Japan Society of Civil Engineers in 2008. The Tsukimi Tunnel (2,184 m), between Hotarudani and Tsukimi-guchi, was bored from both ends between 1927 and 1931; the headings met on 12 December 1930. Fourteen workers died during its construction and are remembered by a memorial stone of 1932 at Tsukimi-guchi. It was the longest tunnel in Minori Prefecture until the Hiwada Road Tunnel opened in 1979. The ruling gradient is 25 ‰ (1 in 40), on the climb between Hotarudani and Tsukimi Onsen. Hattori insisted on this limit, which he considered the most a steam locomotive could manage with a full train, even though it meant boring a long tunnel instead of a cheaper route over the ridge with gradients of 33 ‰. Single-track sections have passing loops at Ōtsuka, Yuzuhara, Kagami-kyō, Nakazawa and Tsukimi-guchi. Rolling stock[edit] 2000 series (since 1996): eight two-car sets (16 cars) in cream with a river-blue stripe, used on all local and rapid trains. They replaced the 1000 series of 1965. 8000 series (since 2019): three three-car sets (9 cars) in navy blue with a gold stripe, used on the Tsukikage. Built by Nishiura Sharyō for 120 km/h, they are limited to the line's 95 km/h. Steam locomotives worked the line until electrification in 1952. The first Tsukikage trains, the 6000 series, ran from 1987 to 2019; set 6001 is preserved at Tsukimi Onsen Station. Kagami River鏡川 The Kagami River in central Harukawa, looking toward the bay, with Kagami Bridge and the castle on Sagimai Hill The Kagami River and its basin in Minori Prefecture Location Country Japan Prefecture Minori Prefecture Municipalities Tsukimi (town), Kagami (town), Harukawa Physical characteristics Source North slope of Mount Tsukimi, about 1,050 m Mouth Minori Bay at Harukawa Length 94 km (96 km in the prefectural register) Basin area 1,620 km² Mean discharge 48.6 m³/s (at Futamata) Main tributary Hosoya River Administration Classification Class A river Dams Ōkubo Dam (1971) Water quality BOD 0.5 mg/L at Futamata (2023) The Kagami River (鏡川, Kagami-gawa) is a Class A river in Minori Prefecture, Japan. It rises on the north slope of Mount Tsukimi and flows 94 km through the towns of Tsukimi and Kagami to Minori Bay at Harukawa, the prefectural capital. With a basin of 1,620 km², about 36% of the prefecture's area, it is the largest river in Minori. Its clear, still pools gave it its name, mirror river , and it is one of the cleanest rivers in western Japan. The river has shaped the history of Harukawa, which was founded beside it as a castle town in 1603. The Great Genbun Flood of 4 October 1739 killed about 1,140 people there and gave rise to the Harukawa Lantern Festival, when about 12,000 lanterns are floated on the river every October. Contents [hide] 1 Course 2 Name and legend 3 Floods and flood control 4 Bridges 5 Ecology and fishing 6 In culture 7 See also 8 Notes 9 References Course[edit] The river rises at about 1,050 m on the north slope of Mount Tsukimi (1,214 m) in the town of Tsukimi. It circles the mountain to the east and then flows south through Tsukimi Valley, the upper valley in which the hot-spring town of Tsukimi Onsen stands at 310 m. Below Hotarudani it enters the town of Kagami and cuts through the Kagami Gorge (鏡峡), a narrow ravine below the old lava cliffs of the mountain, which ends near Kagami-kyō Station. At Futamata ( the fork ) it is joined by its largest tributary, the Hosoya River (細谷川). Mean discharge there is 48.6 m³/s. Below Futamata the valley widens. The river passes the Ōkubo Dam and the yuzu orchards of Yuzuhara, enters Harukawa at Ichinose and Kawamata, and flows past the pottery district of Suyama onto the Harukawa plain. In the city it passes Sagimai Hill, on whose summit Harukawa Castle stands on the left (east) bank 2.6 km from the mouth, and enters Minori Bay through a small delta. The Kagami Line of the Harukawa Railway follows the valley for almost all of its 38.6 km. Before the castle town was built, the village at the mouth was called Kagami-no-tsu, harbor of the Kagami , and the river also gave its name to the ancient Kagami District of Minori Province. A local legend tells of a princess who lost her bronze mirror in the river while crossing at Kagami-no-tsu. Years later a fisherman found the mirror in his net, shining as if new, and it was enshrined at Kagami Shrine in Harukawa, where it is still kept as the shrine's sacred object. Floods and flood control[edit] The lower river has always been prone to floods, especially during the rainy season and the typhoon season. In 1641–1648 the second lord of Harukawa, Asagiri Masatsugu, built the Masatsugu Embankment (正次堤), 3.2 km long, on the left bank to protect the castle town. On 4 October 1739 (Genbun 4), after three days of typhoon rain, the river overtopped the embankment and flooded the lower town, killing about 1,140 people, most of them in Uomachi and Shiomi. The sixth lord, Asagiri Tadatoki, held the first lantern memorial in 1740 and had the embankment raised and strengthened. In September 1934 the Muroto Typhoon again flooded the low ground of Shiomi and Uomachi. The Ōkubo Dam, a 46.5 m concrete gravity dam upstream of Yuzuhara Station in the town of Kagami, was completed in 1971 for flood control and to supply water to Harukawa. On 19 September 2004 a typhoon brought 287.0 mm of rain to Harukawa in one day, the highest daily total on record. The river overflowed in Shiomi, flooding about 2,300 homes, and washed away part of the Kagami Line embankment near Ichinose. The national river office then raised and widened the embankments in Harukawa under an emergency flood-control project completed in 2014. In central Harukawa three road bridges cross the river; from upstream to downstream they are: Road bridges in central Harukawa Bridge Opened Length Notes Sagimai Bridge (鷺舞橋) 1958 372 m Carries Sagimai Avenue Kagami Bridge (鏡橋) 20 March 1932 386 m Nine-span concrete arch; survived the 1945 air raid; widened to 22 m in 1978 Shiomi Bridge (汐見橋) 1959 412 m Replaced a wooden bridge of 1897 During the Lantern Festival the floating lanterns are released just below Kagami Bridge and drift 1.4 km to Shiomi Bridge, where nets stretched across the river collect them. Ecology and fishing[edit] The Kagami River is among the clearest rivers in western Japan: in 2023 its biochemical oxygen demand at Futamata was 0.5 mg/L. The river is known for ayu (sweetfish); the fishing season runs from 1 June to 31 October, and the Kagami River Fisheries Cooperative releases young ayu each spring. Red-spotted masu trout (amago) live in the upper reaches, and fireflies swarm along the stream near Hotarudani in June. Grey herons and kingfishers, the birds of the prefecture and of Harukawa, are common along the lower river. The upper valley and the Kagami Gorge lie in the Tsukimi–Kagami Prefectural Natural Park, designated in 1959. In culture[edit] The river is at the center of Harukawa's main festival, the Harukawa Lantern Festival, held on the second weekend of October. Michiyo Tōno made her debut with the short story Shiomi Bridge (1949), and her novel The River Mirror (1956) tells the story of the 1739 flood and the first lantern memorial. The wavy kawasuji ( river line ) brushwork of Harukawa ware is said to depict the river's currents, and feldspar from its bed is used in the ware's kasumi glaze. Grilled ayu from the river are the basis of kagami-jiru, a clear soup named for its mirror-clear broth (see Cuisine of Harukawa). d: Japanese railway engineer (1873–1941), builder of the Kagami Line
x: Kenzō Hattori服部健三 Personal details Born 2 February 1873Uomachi, Harukawa, Minori Prefecture Died 9 June 1941 (aged 68)Harukawa Education Tokyo Imperial University (civil engineering, 1897) Occupation Railway engineer, company president Career Employers Government Railway Operations Bureau (1897–1922)Kagami Valley Railway (1923–1938) Positions Chief engineer (1923–1931)President (1931–1938) Projects Kagami Line, Futamata Bridge, Tsukimi Tunnel Memorials Statue at Tsukimi-guchi Station (1952) Kenzō Hattori (服部健三, Hattori Kenzō; 2 February 1873 – 9 June 1941) was a Japanese railway engineer from Harukawa who planned and built the Kagami Line of the Harukawa Railway. As chief engineer of the Kagami Valley Railway, the company now called the Harukawa Railway, from 1923 he laid out the 38.6 km route up the valley of the Kagami River to Tsukimi Onsen and designed the Futamata Bridge (1929) and the 2,184 m Tsukimi Tunnel (1931). He was president of the company from 1931 to 1938. He is remembered for insisting on a ruling gradient of 25 ‰ even though it required the long tunnel. After middle school in Harukawa he went to Tokyo in 1890 and studied civil engineering at Tokyo Imperial University, graduating in 1897. Government railways (1897–1922)[edit] On graduating, Hattori joined the government railways. For twenty-five years he worked on mountain lines in central Honshū, surveying routes and supervising the construction of tunnels and bridges. The experience shaped his later views: he saw at first hand how steep gradients limited the loads of steam locomotives and how smoke made long, steeply graded tunnels dangerous for crews. Kagami Valley Railway (1923–1931)[edit] Main article: Kagami Line In 1923, aged 50, Hattori returned home as chief engineer of the newly founded Kagami Valley Railway (鏡谷鉄道). He surveyed the valley in 1923–1924, chose a route that kept close to the Kagami River rather than crossing the hills, and built the line to 1,067 mm gauge from the start. The first 13.5 km, from Harukawa to Kamano, opened on 15 July 1926, and the line reached Yuzuhara on 20 May 1928. Futamata Bridge[edit] For the extension beyond Yuzuhara, Hattori designed the Futamata Bridge, a 218 m steel truss bridge with three truss spans on masonry piers, which crosses the Kagami River just above its confluence with the Hosoya River, below Kagami-kyō Station. He set the piers on bedrock and shaped them to shed flood debris after studying the river's flood marks. The bridge opened with the section to Hotarudani on 3 November 1929 and is still in use. Tsukimi Tunnel and the 25 ‰ rule[edit] The last section, from Hotarudani to Tsukimi Onsen, caused a long dispute. Several directors favored a cheaper route over the ridge with gradients of 33 ‰ and a short summit tunnel of about 600 m. Hattori held that 25 ‰ (1 in 40) was the steepest gradient on which a steam locomotive could reliably haul a full train, and proposed instead a 2,184 m tunnel under a spur of Mount Tsukimi. The board accepted his plan in 1926. The tunnel was bored from both ends from 1927; the headings met on 12 December 1930, and the line opened to Tsukimi Onsen on 4 October 1931. Fourteen workers died during the work. Hattori wrote the inscription of their memorial stone, erected at Tsukimi-guchi in 1932, and described the construction in a paper for the Journal of the Japan Society of Civil Engineers the same year. The tunnel remained the longest in Minori Prefecture until 1979. President (1931–1938)[edit] When the line reached Tsukimi Onsen in 1931, Hattori became president of the Kagami Valley Railway. He guided it through the depression of the early 1930s and promoted Tsukimi Onsen as a resort for city visitors. He retired in 1938, aged 65; the company took its present name, Harukawa Railway, in 1951, ten years after his death. Death and legacy[edit] Hattori died in Harukawa on 9 June 1941, aged 68. In 1952, the year the Kagami Line was electrified, railway employees and residents of Tsukimi erected a bronze statue of him in front of Tsukimi-guchi Station, facing the eastern portal of the tunnel. The ruling gradient of 25 ‰ that he fixed still applies on the line, and the limited express Tsukikage climbs it into the tunnel he designed. The Futamata Bridge was selected as civil engineering heritage in 2008. d: Japanese novelist (1914–1987), author of The River Mirror
x: Michiyo Tōno遠野美千代 Personal information Born 4 August 1914Uomachi, Harukawa, Minori Prefecture Died 19 November 1987 (aged 73)Tsukimi Onsen, Minori Prefecture Occupation Novelist, essayist, teacher Education Minori Normal School (1933) Literary career Active 1949–1987 Genres Novels, historical fiction, short stories, essays Notable works The River Mirror (1956)Heron Castle (1971)Tsukimi Diary (1980) Awards Kōyō Prize (1957) Michiyo Tōno (遠野美千代, Tōno Michiyo; 4 August 1914 – 19 November 1987) was a Japanese novelist and essayist from Harukawa, Minori Prefecture. A schoolteacher until 1946, she made her debut in 1949 and became nationally known with The River Mirror (1956), a novel about the Great Genbun Flood of 1739 and the first lantern memorial on the Kagami River, which won the Kōyō Prize in 1957 and made the Harukawa Lantern Festival famous across Japan. Her later works include the historical novel Heron Castle (1971) and the essay collection Tsukimi Diary (1980). She spent her last fifteen years at Tsukimi Onsen, where the Michiyo Tōno Memorial Hall opened in 1992. Contents [hide] 1 Early life and teaching 2 Debut 3 The River Mirror 4 Later works 5 Tsukimi Onsen years 6 Death 7 Style and themes 8 Legacy 8.1 Michiyo Tōno Memorial Hall 8.2 Literary prize 9 Bibliography 10 See also 11 Notes 12 References Early life and teaching[edit] Tōno was born on 4 August 1914 in Uomachi, the fishing quarter of Harukawa, where her father ran a small fish wholesale business. The date is taken from the family register; in her memoir Tsukimi Diary she gave her year of birth as 1915, and some reference works follow her. She trained as a teacher at Minori Normal School, one of the predecessors of Harukawa University, graduating in 1933, and taught at elementary schools in Harukawa and in Kawamata village from 1933 to 1946. Her school in Shiomi was destroyed in the air raid of 29 July 1945, which killed 1,072 people in the city. She resigned from teaching in 1946 to write. Debut[edit] Tōno's debut was the short story Shiomi Bridge (1949), published in the Harukawa literary magazine Minori Bungaku. It follows a young teacher and a fisherman's son in the burned city after the air raid. A first collection of stories, The Salt Wind, followed in 1953. The River Mirror[edit] The River Mirror (鏡の川, Kagami no kawa, 1956) is set in Harukawa during the Great Genbun Flood of 4 October 1739, which killed about 1,140 people. Its heroine, Osayo, a fisherman's daughter from Uomachi, loses her family in the flood and, a year later, sets the first paper lantern on the river at the memorial ordered in 1740 by the sixth lord, Asagiri Tadatoki. The novel draws on the domain records of the flood and on the legend of the bronze mirror of Kagami Shrine. The book won the Kōyō Prize in 1957 and became a best-seller. It was adapted as a film in 1960, with the lantern scenes filmed at the 1959 festival, and as an eight-part television drama in 1978. The two adaptations brought national attention to the Lantern Festival, and visitor numbers rose sharply in the 1960s. Later works[edit] Lanterns at Low Tide (引き潮の灯, 1962) portrays oyster-farming families of Minori Bay at the time of the plans for the bay reclamation of 1961–1966, which they opposed. The Potter's Daughter (1966) is set among the kilns of Suyama in the 1930s; readers took it as a portrait of the potter Hanae Ishizuka, but Tōno denied this. From 1965 to 1972 Tōno lectured on modern Japanese literature at Harukawa University. In 1971 she published Heron Castle (鷺舞城, Sagimai-jō), a historical novel about Asagiri Tadatoki and the fire that destroyed the keep of Harukawa Castle after a lightning strike on 15 June 1749. It is still sold at the castle's museum shop. Tsukimi Onsen years[edit] In 1972 Tōno moved to the hot-spring town of Tsukimi Onsen, at the end of the Kagami Line, and lived in an annex of the inn Seiryūkan (清流館) beside the river. There she wrote Valley of the Moon (1976), a novel set in the upper Kagami valley, and Tsukimi Diary (月見日記, Tsukimi nikki, 1980), essays on her childhood in Uomachi, her teaching years and life in the valley below Mount Tsukimi. She never married. Death[edit] Tōno died at Tsukimi Onsen on 19 November 1987, aged 73. Her grave is at Kōun-ji in Harukawa. A last collection of stories, The Last Lantern, was published in 1988. Style and themes[edit] Almost all of Tōno's fiction is set in Harukawa and the Kagami valley, and water runs through it: the river, the bay, floods, tides and the lanterns set adrift for the dead. Her heroines are mostly ordinary working women, fishermen's daughters, teachers and kiln workers, and her historical novels tell the story of the Asagiri domain from below rather than from the castle. Critics praised her plain, unhurried prose and her use of the Harukawa dialect in dialogue. Kaneda describes her as the writer who taught Harukawa to remember its river . Legacy[edit] Michiyo Tōno Memorial Hall[edit] The Michiyo Tōno Memorial Hall (遠野美千代記念館) opened in Tsukimi Onsen in 1992, near the Seiryūkan. It displays her manuscripts, letters, desk and personal library, a reconstruction of her study at the inn, and material on the film and television adaptations of The River Mirror. Literary prize[edit] The city of Harukawa has awarded the Michiyo Tōno Literary Prize (遠野美千代文学賞) every year since 1989 for unpublished short fiction. The award ceremony is held each October in the week of the Lantern Festival. x: Minori Bayみのり湾 Oyster rafts on Minori Bay in the morning Minori Bay in Minori Prefecture Geography Location Minori Prefecture, Japan Main inflow Kagami River Area 286 km² Maximum depth 38 m Average depth 17 m Mouth 7.2 km wide, between Cape Okitsu and the Uchiura Peninsula Islands Kasumi Island, Sagi Island Settlements Harukawa, Okitsu Use Oyster rafts about 1,920 Oyster harvest 6,300 t shucked (2023) Ports Minori Port, Uomachi fishing port Minori Bay (みのり湾, Minori-wan) is a bay on the coast of Minori Prefecture, Japan. The prefectural capital, Harukawa, stands at its head, where the Kagami River enters the bay. The bay covers 286 km², with an average depth of 17 m and a maximum depth of 38 m, and opens to the sea through a 7.2 km wide mouth between Cape Okitsu and the Uchiura Peninsula. Sheltered and fed with nutrients by the river, it is one of the prefecture's main fishing grounds, known for farmed oysters and sea bream. Contents [hide] 1 Geography 2 Islands 3 Fisheries 4 Reclamation 5 Transport and recreation 6 See also 7 Notes 8 References Geography[edit] The bay is a drowned valley, shallow near its head and deepening toward the mouth. The Kagami River, which drains 1,620 km², is by far the largest of the streams that flow into it. The north shore, from central Harukawa to Minori Port, is largely built up, with the fishing port of Uomachi, the shipyard on reclaimed land, the seaside park and aquarium at Minori-kōen and the beach of Sakurahama. The hilly Uchiura Peninsula closes off the inner bay off central Harukawa; its terraced slopes grow yuzu, and the Jōmon-period Uchiura Shell Mound shows that people have gathered shellfish on its shore for about 5,000 years. The opposite side of the mouth is Cape Okitsu, in the city of Okitsu. Islands[edit] Islands of Minori Bay Island Area Population Notes Kasumi Island (霞島) 5.8 km² 1,240 Part of Harukawa; ferry 35 minutes from Minori Port Sagi Island (鷺島) 0.4 km² 0 Grey heron colony; wildlife reserve Kasumi Island, the larger island, belongs to the city of Harukawa and lives from fishing, sea bream farming and citrus; its name, mist island , refers to the morning haze that often hides it from the city. Ferries from Minori Port take 35 minutes. The small, wooded Sagi Island is uninhabited and is a prefectural wildlife reserve because of its colony of grey herons, the prefectural bird; landing is not allowed during the nesting season from March to July. Fisheries[edit] Oyster farming in the bay began in 1878. Today about 1,920 rafts are moored in the inner bay and off the Uchiura Peninsula, and the harvest in 2023 was 6,300 tonnes of shucked oysters. The season runs from November to March, when the oysters are used in Minori kaki-nabe and other dishes of the local cuisine. Red sea bream (madai) are raised in net pens, mainly around Kasumi Island, and are the main ingredient of tai-yuzu meshi, Harukawa's signature dish. The catch is landed at Uomachi, whose central fish market opened in 1956. In the summer of 2017 a red tide of plankton spread through the inner bay, killing farmed sea bream and oysters and costing the fisheries about ¥1.2 billion; it was the worst such event on record in the bay. The prefecture has since monitored the water weekly from June to September. Reclamation[edit] Parts of Uomachi and Shiomi were reclaimed from the bay during the Edo period. The largest project came in 1961–1966, when 2.4 km² of the north shore was reclaimed for the Harukawa Shipyard of Minori Heavy Industries. Oyster fishermen opposed the work, which destroyed some of their best grounds, and a lawsuit filed in 1965 was settled in 1968 with ¥380 million in compensation. The project was promoted by the mayor of Harukawa, Tetsuo Saeki, and remains the most disputed part of his record. Transport and recreation[edit] The Bayside Line of the Harukawa Railway runs 16.2 km along the north shore from Harukawa Central Station to Minori Port, from where ferries sail to Kasumi Island. The Minori Bay Aquarium, opened in 1997 in the seaside park beside Minori-kōen Station, had 466,000 visitors in FY2024. During the Harukawa Lantern Festival, 4,000 fireworks are launched over the bay on the Sunday evening. Opened in 1983, it holds about 9,600 works, including the largest public collection of Harukawa ware. It received 186,000 visitors in fiscal year 2024.
