The museum opened on 3 November 1983, Culture Day. It closed in April 2017 for renovation, which renewed the air conditioning, lighting and earthquake protection of the display cases, and reopened on 3 November 2018, its 35th anniversary. Architecture[edit] The building was designed by the architect Shūji Kamiya (神谷修二). It is a long, low structure of exposed concrete with long glass walls that face a shallow reflecting pond, laid out so that the galleries do not compete with the castle walls beside them. The galleries are on two floors, with a glass corridor along the pond. Collection[edit] The collection of about 9,600 works covers Japanese painting, Western art, prints and the crafts of Minori. Its 1,240 pieces of Harukawa ware range from pieces of the Edo-period domain kiln and export ware to contemporary work. x: Minori Prefectureみのり県 Minori Prefecture Overview Country Japan Capital Harukawa Former province Minori Province (実野国) Established 14 November 1871 (as 実野県) Present name 1 April 1971 Government Governor Hiroshi Takemura (since 2017) Municipalities 22 (9 cities, 11 towns, 2 villages) Districts 6 Area and population Area 4,512.8 km² Population 1,086,400 (estimate, 1 October 2025) Density about 241/km² Highest point Mount Hiwada (1,477 m) Largest river Kagami River Symbols Flower Yuzu blossom Bird Grey heron Tree Japanese black pine Minori Prefecture (みのり県, Minori-ken) is a prefecture of Japan. Its capital and largest city is Harukawa, on Minori Bay at the mouth of the Kagami River. The prefecture had an estimated 1,086,400 inhabitants on 1 October 2025 and covers 4,512.8 km², giving a density of about 241 people per km². It corresponds to the former Minori Province and was ruled during the Edo period mainly by the Asagiri clan from Harukawa Castle. It is known for Harukawa ware, yuzu, oysters and sea bream, shipbuilding, and the hot springs and mountain scenery of Tsukimi Onsen and Mount Tsukimi. Contents [hide] 1 Name 2 History 3 Geography 4 Municipalities 5 Economy 6 Transport 7 Culture 8 Tourism 9 See also 10 Notes 11 References Name[edit] The prefecture takes its name from Minori Province (実野国), one of the provinces of ancient Japan. The name is usually connected with minori (実り), ripening or harvest . When the prefecture was created in 1871 it was written with the province's characters as 実野県, but the reading Minori of 実野 is irregular, and the name was often misread as Jitsuno or Saneno , even in official correspondence. To mark the prefecture's centenary, the official name was changed to the hiragana form みのり県 on 1 April 1971. The change followed a 1969 survey in which most residents favored the hiragana spelling, and because a prefecture's name can only be changed by law, it required an act of the National Diet, passed in 1970. The prefecture is thus one of the few in Japan whose name is written in hiragana rather than kanji. History[edit] See also: History of Harukawa, Asagiri clan Minori Province was established in the 8th century; its districts included Kagami District, named after the river. From the 1400s to 1600 the south of the province was ruled by the Uchiura clan from Kurayama Castle. After the Battle of Sekigahara (1600), Asagiri Tadamasa received the province with an assessed yield of 186,000 koku and in 1603 began Harukawa Castle and its castle town. In 1651 a branch family, the Uchiura Asagiri, received 10,000 koku, forming the small Uchiura Domain. When the domains were abolished in 1871, the Harukawa Domain became Harukawa Prefecture. On 14 November 1871 it was merged with Uchiura Prefecture, the former branch domain, and Kitano Prefecture, formed from former shogunate lands in the north, to create 実野県, with Harukawa as its capital. In the 20th century the prefecture developed shipbuilding and machinery around Harukawa; the city was badly damaged in an air raid on 29 July 1945. The Tsukimi–Kagami Prefectural Natural Park was designated in 1959, and in 1971 the prefecture adopted its present name and opened Minori Airport. Mergers between 2003 and 2006 reduced the number of municipalities from 41 to the present 22. Geography[edit] The north of the prefecture is mountainous. The highest point is Mount Hiwada (日和田山, 1,477 m) on the northern border; Mount Tsukimi (1,214 m), a dormant volcano about 32 km north-east of Harukawa, is the best known but only the second highest. The largest river, the Kagami River, rises on Mount Tsukimi and flows 94 km to Minori Bay; its basin of 1,620 km² covers about 36% of the prefecture. The plains around Harukawa and Kitano hold most of the population. The south of the prefecture faces Minori Bay (286 km²), entered between Cape Okitsu and the Uchiura Peninsula, with Kasumi Island and Sagi Island. The coast has a humid subtropical climate; Harukawa has an annual mean temperature of 16.5 °C (see Climate of Harukawa), while the mountains of the north are much cooler and receive snow in winter. The Tsukimi–Kagami Prefectural Natural Park (1959) covers Mount Tsukimi, the Tsukimi Valley and the Kagami Gorge. Municipalities[edit] The prefecture has 22 municipalities: 9 cities, 11 towns and 2 villages, the towns and villages grouped in 6 districts. Kagami and Tsukimi, the two towns of the upper Kagami valley, form Kagami District. Economy[edit] The prefecture's economy is centered on Harukawa, whose gross city product of ¥1.68 trillion (FY2022) is about two-fifths of the prefectural total (see Economy of Harukawa). The main industries are shipbuilding, at the Harukawa Shipyard of Minori Heavy Industries; machinery, led by Kagami Precision; and railway rolling stock, built by Nishiura Sharyō, which made the 8000 series of the Tsukikage. Harukawa ware, a nationally designated Traditional Craft since 1979, was worth ¥2.1 billion in 2024. Minori is the third-largest producer of yuzu in Japan, with 4,350 tonnes in 2023 from about 520 ha (see Yuzu cultivation in Minori). Minori Bay yields about 6,300 tonnes of shucked oysters a year from about 1,920 rafts, along with farmed sea bream. Minori Bank, founded in 1897, is the main regional bank. Transport[edit] The Harukawa Railway (HaruTetsu) runs the prefecture's main local railway: the Kagami Line (38.6 km, 14 stations) from Harukawa Central Station up the Kagami valley to Tsukimi Onsen, and the Bayside Line (16.2 km, 9 stations) along the bay to Minori Port. Its contactless card is HaruCa. Minori Airport, opened in 1971 in Nishiura, 22 km south-west of Harukawa, handles domestic flights. The Minori Expressway crosses the prefecture, and the Hiwada Road Tunnel (1979) links the north with the neighboring prefecture. Ferries sail from Minori Port to Kasumi Island in 35 minutes. Culture[edit] The best-known event is the Harukawa Lantern Festival, held since 1740 in memory of the victims of the 1739 flood and now on the second weekend of October. Harukawa ware is made mainly in Suyama, where the Kamano Pottery Fair is held in front of Kamano Station on the first weekend of May. Tsukimi washi, a handmade paper from the town of Tsukimi, is used for the festival's lanterns. Local dishes include tai-yuzu meshi (sea bream rice with yuzu) and Minori kaki-nabe (oyster hot pot) (see Cuisine of Harukawa). The Minori Prefectural Museum of Art (1983) and Harukawa University (1949) are both in Harukawa. The novelist Michiyo Tōno and the potter Hanae Ishizuka are the prefecture's best-known artists. Tourism[edit] Harukawa alone received 6.5 million tourist visitors in 2025. The main attractions are Harukawa Castle, whose keep had 512,000 visitors in FY2024; the Lantern Festival (380,000 in 2025); the Minori Bay Aquarium; and Tsukimi Onsen, with 23 inns and 612,000 overnight stays in 2024. The Tsukimi Ropeway (1968) climbs Mount Tsukimi, and the autumn colors of the mountain and the Kagami Gorge attract visitors from mid-October to mid-November. x: Mount Tsukimi月見山 Mount Tsukimi seen across rice terraces from Kagami Town Location in Minori Prefecture Geography Elevation 1,214 m(1,216 m before 2014) Location Tsukimi Town, Minori Prefecture, Japan Distance about 32 km north-east of central Harukawa Summit Meigetsu-dake (明月岳) Rank 2nd highest in the prefecture Geology Type Stratovolcano (dormant) Rock Andesite Last eruption about 24,000 years ago Climbing Easiest route Tsukimi Ropeway and Sanjō trail (1 h 10 min) Protected area Tsukimi–Kagami Prefectural Natural Park (1959) Mount Tsukimi (月見山, Tsukimi-yama, moon-viewing mountain ) is a dormant stratovolcano in the town of Tsukimi, Minori Prefecture, Japan, about 32 km north-east of central Harukawa. At 1,214 m it is the second-highest peak in the prefecture after Mount Hiwada (1,477 m), but its rounded cone, visible from most of the Harukawa plain, makes it the best-known mountain in Minori. The Kagami River rises on its north slope, and the hot-spring town of Tsukimi Onsen lies at its southern foot. Contents [hide] 1 Geography and geology 2 Name 3 Religion 4 Climbing 4.1 Ropeway 5 Seasons 6 Natural park 7 See also 8 Notes 9 References Geography and geology[edit] Mount Tsukimi is an andesite stratovolcano built by eruptions that began about 300,000 years ago. The summit, Meigetsu-dake (明月岳), is a lava dome from the last eruptive stage; the most recent eruption, about 24,000 years ago, produced lava flows on the south-west flank that now form the cliffs above the Kagami Gorge. Because it has not erupted in the last 10,000 years, it is not on the national list of active volcanoes; the heat of the old magma body is thought to feed the springs of Tsukimi Onsen. The Kagami River rises at about 1,050 m on the north slope and circles the mountain to the east before flowing south through Tsukimi Valley. The summit is about 7.5 °C colder than Harukawa on average, and snow covers the upper slopes from December to March. Beech forest grows above about 900 m, with mixed maple and oak forest below. Name[edit] The mountain is named for the moon. Seen from Harukawa Castle, the full moon of the 15th night of the 8th lunar month, the traditional night for moon viewing, rises over its rounded summit, and the Asagiri lords held moon-viewing parties in the castle keep to watch it. The summit's name, Meigetsu-dake, bright-moon peak , has the same origin. Religion[edit] The summit has been a place of mountain worship since at least the Heian period. The upper shrine of Tsukimi Shrine stands on Meigetsu-dake, and its lower shrine is in Tsukimi Onsen. The Asagiri lords of Harukawa prayed there for rain in years of drought and rebuilt the upper shrine in 1702. The climbing season opens with a ceremony at the upper shrine on the first Sunday of May. Climbing[edit] Pilgrims to the upper shrine used the Omote trail from the Edo period, and in the early 20th century the mountain became a favorite outing for students from Harukawa. The arrival of the Kagami Line at Tsukimi Onsen in 1931 brought day hikers from the city, and the first Meigetsu Hut was built in 1932; the present hut dates from 1987. On clear days the summit looks south over the Harukawa plain to Minori Bay and north to Mount Hiwada. Three main trails reach the summit. The Meigetsu Hut, just below the summit, is staffed from May to November and has about 40 beds. Ropeway[edit] The Tsukimi Ropeway (月見ロープウェイ), opened in 1968, climbs 2,140 m from Kōgen Station (580 m) to Sanjō Station (1,020 m) in 9 minutes. A round trip costs ¥2,200 for adults (one way ¥1,300; children half price). Cars leave every 20 minutes. Tsukimi Bus route 5 runs from Tsukimi Onsen Station, the stop for the Tsukikage limited express, to Kōgen Station in 25 minutes (¥480), every 40 minutes; the last bus leaves the station at 16:20. The ropeway carries about 240,000 passengers a year, most of them in October and November. Seasons[edit] Azaleas flower on the upper slopes in late May. In autumn the leaves turn first at the summit, from mid to late October, and the colors move down to Tsukimi Onsen by early to mid November; the ropeway is busiest during these weeks. Winter ascents need crampons, and the ropeway runs year-round for views of the snow-covered summit. Natural park[edit] The mountain is the center of the Tsukimi–Kagami Prefectural Natural Park, designated in 1959. The park covers about 18,400 ha, including the summit area, Tsukimi Valley and the Kagami Gorge. Japanese serow, Asian black bears and copper pheasants live in its forests, and hikers are advised to carry bear bells. d: Mayor of Harukawa from 1951 to 1967
x: Tetsuo Saeki佐伯哲夫 Mayor of Harukawa In office April 1951 – April 1967 (four terms) Preceded as deputy mayor 1947–1951 Personal details Born 17 May 1902Kawamata village, Minori Prefecture (now Harukawa) Died 8 March 1979 (aged 76)Harukawa Party Independent Alma mater Kyoto Imperial University (civil engineering) Profession Civil engineer Honors Honorary citizen of Harukawa (1968) Tetsuo Saeki (佐伯哲夫, Saeki Tetsuo; 17 May 1902 – 8 March 1979) was a Japanese civil engineer and politician who served as mayor of Harukawa, Minori Prefecture, for four terms from 1951 to 1967. A prefectural engineer before the Second World War, he became deputy mayor in 1947 and directed the rebuilding of the city after the air raid of 1945. As mayor he built the 50 m wide Sagimai Avenue, carried out the 1954 merger with four villages, brought Harukawa University to its Sagimai Campus and led the citizens' campaign that rebuilt the keep of Harukawa Castle in 1966. His support for the reclamation of Minori Bay for the shipyard, opposed by oyster fishermen, remains the most disputed part of his record. Contents [hide] 1 Early life and career 2 Deputy mayor (1947–1951) 3 Mayor (1951–1967) 3.1 Reconstruction and growth 3.2 The castle keep 4 Reclamation controversy 5 Later life and legacy 6 See also 7 Notes 8 References Early life and career[edit] Saeki was born on 17 May 1902 in Kawamata, a farming village on the Kagami River north-east of Harukawa, the second son of a rice farmer who sat on the village assembly. He went to middle school in Harukawa and graduated in civil engineering from Kyoto Imperial University in 1925. From 1925 to 1945 he worked as a civil engineer for the prefectural government. He worked on roads and river works, including the repair and raising of the embankments of the Kagami River after the flood of 1934, and by 1943 headed the prefecture's river section. After the air raid of 29 July 1945, which burned 38 % of the urban area and killed 1,072 people, he led the prefecture's survey of the damage. Deputy mayor (1947–1951)[edit] Saeki joined the city as deputy mayor in 1947. His reconstruction plan replaced the narrow streets of the burned center with a grid of wider roads, the most important of which was Sagimai Avenue (鷺舞通り), a 50 m wide avenue from the station square past the castle, built between 1949 and 1958 and designed as a firebreak; he had it lined with ginkgo trees, which resist fire. In October 1947 he revived the Harukawa Lantern Festival, suspended since 1944, and the floating lanterns that year were dedicated to the dead of the air raid as well as to the victims of the 1739 flood. Mayor (1951–1967)[edit] Saeki was elected mayor in April 1951 as an independent and re-elected in 1955, 1959 and 1963. Mayoral elections won by Tetsuo Saeki Election Date Votes Share Candidates 1st April 1951 38,412 52.3 % 3 2nd April 1955 61,950 61.8 % 2 3rd April 1959 70,233 64.0 % 2 4th April 1963 64,871 54.1 % 3 Reconstruction and growth[edit] In 1951 he offered Harukawa University, founded in 1949, the site of former army barracks next to the Minori Higher Commercial School for its main campus, which opened that year as the Sagimai Campus. He negotiated the merger of 1 October 1954 with the four villages of Kawamata, his birthplace, Ichinose, Uchiura and Sakurahama, which raised the population from 171,346 (1950 census) to 238,517 (1955). He pressed the Harukawa Railway to build a line along the bay, and the Bayside Line opened to Minori Port on 1 October 1962. The castle keep[edit] The reconstruction of the castle keep, demolished in 1874, was Saeki's best-remembered project. In 1962 he launched the One Tile, One Citizen campaign, in which donors of ¥1,000 or more could write their names on a roof tile. About 40 % of the cost of ¥214 million came from donations by about 71,000 citizens and 640 companies and associations. The reinforced-concrete keep opened on 3 November 1966. Reclamation controversy[edit] Saeki supported the plan of the city and the prefecture to reclaim 2.4 km² of Minori Bay between 1961 and 1966 for the expansion of the Harukawa Shipyard, the city's largest private employer. He argued that the shipyard would otherwise move elsewhere. The oyster fishermen of the bay, who had farmed oysters there since 1878, objected that the reclamation would destroy tidal flats and spawning grounds and change the currents over their rafts. Protest boats blocked the start of the work in 1961, and in 1965 a group of oyster fishermen sued the city and the prefecture. The narrow result of the 1963 election was widely attributed to the dispute. The lawsuit was settled in 1968, after Saeki had left office, with compensation of ¥380 million. Historians of the city have credited the reclamation with securing several thousand industrial jobs, but also with the loss of most of the inner bay's tidal flats. Later life and legacy[edit] Saeki did not stand in the election of April 1967 and retired at the age of 64. The city made him an honorary citizen in 1968. In retirement he chaired the association that maintained the keep museum's collection and published a memoir, A City from the Ashes (1972). He died in Harukawa on 8 March 1979, aged 76. A bronze bust of Saeki was unveiled in 1982 at the west end of Sagimai Avenue. He is generally regarded as the builder of postwar Harukawa: the avenue, the merged city, the university campus and the rebuilt keep all date from his years in office. The reclamation has kept his reputation contested, and the 1968 settlement is still cited in debates over the bay. The three five-car 6000 series sets built for it each included a panoramic lounge car called Moonlight that was open to all passengers. Trains at first took 52 minutes, and by the early 1990s there were six round trips a day. After track improvements in 1994 raised the line's limit to 95 km/h, the journey fell to 47 minutes. Since 2019[edit] The 8000 series entered service on 16 March 2019, the day after the last run of the 6000 series, and brought the present 39-minute timing. During the pandemic the service was cut to five round trips a day from April to June 2020. The added stop at Tsukimi-guchi from 14 November 2026 will make the journey 41 minutes. They have aluminum-alloy bodies painted navy blue with a gold stripe and seat 118 passengers: 24 in the Premium car (car 1), 38 in car 2, which also has two wheelchair spaces and a multipurpose toilet, and 56 in car 3, which has a luggage area. The trains were designed for 120 km/h because, when they were ordered, HaruTetsu planned to raise the speed limit between Kamano and Kagami-kyō to 110 km/h. That plan, estimated to cost ¥6.8 billion, was postponed indefinitely in 2017, and the 8000 series therefore runs at no more than the line's 95 km/h. The extra power is used instead for faster acceleration and on the 25 ‰ climb to Tsukimi Onsen, which is the main reason the journey is eight minutes shorter than with the 6000 series. Premium car[edit] The Premium car (プレミアム) is car 1, at the Tsukimi Onsen end of the train. Its 24 leather seats are arranged two plus one, with footrests and reading lights, and a panoramic window behind the driver's cab gives a forward view of the valley, the Futamata Bridge and the approach to the Tsukimi Tunnel. It costs ¥700 on top of the limited express surcharge, also for children, and is often sold out on weekends in the autumn-color season and during the Lantern Festival. Fares[edit] The limited express surcharge depends on the distance traveled on the Tsukikage: ¥520 for up to 25 km and ¥760 for 26 km or more (children ¥260 and ¥380), charged on top of the ordinary fare. On peak dates (10–12 October 2026, 28 December 2026 – 6 January 2027, 27 April – 6 May 2027 and 8–17 August 2027) it is ¥200 higher, and a surcharge bought on board costs ¥260 more. A trip from Harukawa Central to Tsukimi Onsen therefore costs ¥730 + ¥760 = ¥1,490, or ¥2,190 in the Premium car. Reservations open at 10:00 one month before the travel date, at staffed stations, from reserved-seat ticket machines and online. A HaruCa card touched at the gates pays only the fare, but the surcharge can be paid from its balance at reserved-seat machines, and since 2024 Mobile HaruCa can also hold a ticketless Tsukikage seat reservation. Name[edit] Tsukikage is a literary word for moonlight or the light of the moon (literally moon's shadow ). The name refers to Mount Tsukimi (1,214 m), the moon-viewing mountain over whose rounded summit the harvest moon rises when seen from Harukawa Castle. It was chosen in 1986 from 3,412 entries in a public naming contest. The moon theme continued in the Moonlight lounge car of the 6000 series. x: Tsukimi Onsen月見温泉 Inns along the stream at dusk Location in Minori Prefecture Location Town Tsukimi Town (population 6,840), Minori Prefecture Elevation 310 m Valley Tsukimi Valley (upper Kagami River) Springs Sources 41 Temperature 42–68.2 °C Flow about 4,800 L/min Type Sodium chloride–hydrogen carbonate Tourism Discovered 807 (legend) Inns and hotels 23 (2025) Overnight stays 612,000 (2024) Access Kagami Line, Tsukimi Onsen Station (terminus, 38.6 km from Harukawa Central) Tsukimi Onsen (月見温泉) is a hot-spring town in the town of Tsukimi, Minori Prefecture, Japan. It lies at an elevation of 310 m in Tsukimi Valley, the upper valley of the Kagami River, at the southern foot of Mount Tsukimi. Its 41 sources yield about 4,800 liters a minute of sodium chloride–hydrogen carbonate water at 42 to 68.2 °C. The town is the terminus of the Kagami Line of the Harukawa Railway, 38.6 km from Harukawa Central Station, and had 23 inns and hotels in 2025 and 612,000 overnight stays in 2024. Contents [hide] 1 History 2 Springs and baths 3 Town 4 Access 5 Culture 5.1 Michiyo Tōno 5.2 Festivals 5.3 Food 6 See also 7 Notes 8 References History[edit] According to local legend, the springs were discovered in 807 by a traveling monk who saw a wounded grey heron bathing in a warm pool beside the river and recovering its strength; the source he found is still called Sagi-no-yu, heron's bath . For centuries the springs were used by farmers of the valley for hot-spring cures (tōji) in the slack winter months. In 1660 the 3rd lord of Harukawa, Asagiri Tadakiyo, built a private bathhouse for the lords, the Goten-yu (御殿湯), over the hottest source, and the village became a stop for officials and pilgrims to the shrine on Mount Tsukimi. The Goten-yu was dismantled after the domain was abolished in 1871. The modern resort began with the railway. The Kagami Line reached Tsukimi Onsen through the Tsukimi Tunnel on 4 October 1931, cutting the journey from Harukawa from a day on foot to under two hours. The number of inns grew from seven in 1930 to 21 in 1937, and the public bath Tsukimi Sōyu (月見総湯) was rebuilt in wood in 1931. After the Second World War the Tsukimi Ropeway (1968) made the town a popular destination for group tours, and after the limited express Tsukikage began running in 1987, overnight stays peaked at about 870,000 in 1991. They fell during the 1990s and 2000s, then recovered with individual travelers; the second public bath, Kogane-yu (こがね湯), opened in 2006. Springs and baths[edit] The springs are heated by the old magma body beneath Mount Tsukimi. The water is clear and slightly salty and is said to leave the skin smooth; local inns call it beauty water . Most inns have their own baths, and two public bathhouses and a free foot bath in front of the station are open to day visitors. The inns line both banks of the stream for about 1 km above the station, with a shopping street of souvenir shops, soba restaurants and washi makers; Tsukimi washi, made in the town, is used for the lanterns of the Harukawa Lantern Festival. The lower shrine of Tsukimi Shrine stands at the head of the street. The surrounding valleys grow Tsukimi yuzu , a registered Geographical Indication since 2019 (see Yuzu cultivation in Minori). The town's annual mean temperature is 13.8 °C, about 2.7 °C cooler than Harukawa. Access[edit] Tsukimi Onsen Station is the terminus of the Kagami Line, 38.6 km from Harukawa Central, with 2,870 boardings a day in fiscal 2025. Local trains from Harukawa Central take 63 minutes and run hourly beyond Kamano; hourly rapid trains take 55 minutes. The limited express Tsukikage takes 39 minutes, stopping only at Shiromachi, Kamano and Kagami-kyō, with 7 northbound and 8 southbound trains on weekdays and 9 and 10 on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. The fare is ¥730 (¥715 with HaruCa), plus a ¥760 limited express surcharge on the Tsukikage, ¥1,490 in all. The two-day Tsukimi Onsen Yukemuri Ticket (¥2,800) covers a return journey with Tsukikage seats both ways, one entry to Tsukimi Sōyu or Kogane-yu (Kogane-yu since 1 July 2026) and a ¥500 voucher for shops in the town. Tsukikage set 6001, of the 6000 series that ran the service from 1987 to 2019, is preserved beside the station. Tsukimi Bus route 5 runs from the station to Kōgen Station of the Tsukimi Ropeway in 25 minutes (¥480, every 40 minutes). Culture[edit] Michiyo Tōno[edit] The novelist Michiyo Tōno, author of The River Mirror (1956), lived in Tsukimi Onsen from 1972 in an annex of the inn Seiryūkan (清流館), where she wrote the essays of Tsukimi Diary (1980). She died there on 19 November 1987. The Michiyo Tōno Memorial Hall opened near the Seiryūkan in 1992 and displays her manuscripts, desk and library. Festivals[edit] On the night of the September full moon the town holds its Moon Festival, with moon-viewing at the square in front of Tsukimi Sōyu, offerings of rice dumplings and Tsukimi yuzu, and lanterns along the stream. On the winter solstice the inns and public baths float whole yuzu in their baths, a custom that draws many day visitors from Harukawa. Food[edit] The town's speciality is onsen yu-soba, buckwheat noodles from the Tsukimi highlands rinsed in hot-spring water, served at about ten shops. c: Railway bridges and tunnels in Minori Prefecture
x: Tsukimi Tunnel月見トンネル Mount Tsukimi in Minori Prefecture Line Kagami Line Location Between Hotarudani and Tsukimi-guchi, Tsukimi Length 2,184 m Track Single Built 1927–1931 Breakthrough 12 December 1930 Opened 4 October 1931 Engineer Kenzō Hattori The Tsukimi Tunnel (月見トンネル, Tsukimi tonneru) is a 2,184-metre single-track railway tunnel on the Kagami Line of the Harukawa Railway, between Hotarudani and Tsukimi-guchi stations in the town of Tsukimi, Minori Prefecture. It carries the line under a spur of Mount Tsukimi on the climb to Tsukimi Onsen, the section with the line's ruling gradient of 25 ‰. The tunnel was built from 1927 to 1931 for the Kagami Valley Railway under its chief engineer Kenzō Hattori, who preferred it to a cheaper route over the ridge with gradients of 33 ‰. It was bored from both ends, the headings met on 12 December 1930, and it opened with the last section of the line on 4 October 1931. Fourteen workers died during construction; a memorial stone with an inscription by Hattori was erected at Tsukimi-guchi in 1932. It was built for the 1,067 mm gauge and electrified in 1952. It was the longest tunnel in Minori Prefecture until the Hiwada Road Tunnel opened in 1979. The limited express Tsukikage passes through it in about two minutes. d: Growing of yuzu citrus in Minori Prefecture, Japan
x: Yuzu cultivation in Minoriみのり県のユズ栽培 Terraced yuzu orchard on the Uchiura Peninsula above Minori Bay Crop Yuzu (Citrus junos) Region Minori Prefecture, Japan Introduced 1688 (by order of the 4th lord Asagiri Tadanobu) Production 4,350 t (2023), 3rd in Japan Record crop 4,480 t (2019) Area about 520 ha (2020) Farming households 1,140 (2020) Main areas Uchiura Peninsula, Kagami Town (Yuzuhara), Tsukimi Town Varieties Local seedling lines, Minori Kogane (2011) Geographical Indication Tsukimi yuzu (2019) Yuzu cultivation in Minori is the growing of yuzu (柚子, Citrus junos), a sour, fragrant East Asian citrus, in Minori Prefecture, Japan. The prefecture produced 4,350 tonnes of yuzu in 2023, the third-largest crop of any prefecture, from about 520 hectares farmed by 1,140 households. Yuzu has been grown on a large scale since 1688, when the domain ordered every farming household to plant three trees. The yuzu blossom is the prefectural flower, and the fruit flavors most of the dishes in the cuisine of Harukawa. Contents [hide] 1 History 2 Growing areas 3 Varieties 4 Season 5 Production 6 Processing and uses 7 Geographical Indication 8 Research 9 See also 10 Notes 11 References History[edit] See also: History of Harukawa, Asagiri clan Yuzu grew in the region before the Edo period, but only as scattered garden trees. After the Tenna famine of 1681–82, the 4th lord of the Asagiri clan, Asagiri Tadanobu, looked for crops that would grow on slopes unfit for rice. In 1688 he ordered every farming household in the domain to plant three yuzu trees. Yuzu is hardy, tolerates cold better than most citrus, and its juice could be stored as a vinegar; by the mid-18th century yuzu vinegar and salted peel were shipped from Harukawa to Osaka. In the Meiji era farmers on the Uchiura Peninsula built stone terraces above Minori Bay for yuzu orchards. Demand grew after the Second World War with the market for processed foods, and in 1974 the prefectural agricultural cooperative opened a juice and peel processing plant at Yuzuhara in the town of Kagami. Since the 2000s exports of juice and peel to Europe and North America have also grown. Growing areas[edit] Most orchards lie on sloping, well-drained land between about 50 and 500 m above sea level. The three main areas are the terraces of the Uchiura Peninsula in Harukawa, the middle Kagami River valley around Yuzuhara in Kagami Town, and the valleys of Tsukimi Town below Mount Tsukimi, whose cooler climate gives thicker, more fragrant peel. Seedling trees are long-lived and very fragrant but thorny, and take ten or more years to bear; a local saying holds that yuzu takes eighteen years . Grafted trees bear after four or five years. Minori Kogane (みのり黄金, Minori gold ) is a less thorny, early-bearing variety bred by the Minori Prefectural Fruit Tree Experiment Station and the Yuzuhara Field Station of Harukawa University, and registered in 2011. Its short thorns make harvesting faster and reduce scarring of the fruit, and grafted trees begin bearing in their third year. It covered about 15 % of the prefecture's yuzu area in 2023. Season[edit] The yuzu year in Minori Period Work in the orchards January–March Pruning; frost protection; planting and grafting May Flowering June–July Fruit thinning; pest and disease control August–September Harvest of green yuzu (for yuzu kosho and juice) October–December Harvest of yellow yuzu, peaking in early November Winter solstice Yuzu baths at Tsukimi Onsen and in homes The green yuzu harvest supplies the sharp, aromatic peel used for yuzu kosho. The main harvest of ripe yellow yuzu runs from October to December and peaks in early November; the fruit is picked by hand with clippers because of the thorns. Production[edit] Production has varied between about 3,600 and 4,500 tonnes a year since 2014. Yuzu trees tend to alternate heavy and light crops, and the weather causes larger swings: a late spring frost cut the 2016 crop to 3,640 t, and the heavy rain of July 2018 damaged orchards and reduced that year's crop to 3,710 t. The record crop of 4,480 t came in 2019. The fruit is pressed for juice, and the peel is frozen, dried or candied. The main products are yuzu kosho (a paste of green peel, chili and salt), yuzu ponzu, yuzu-shu liqueur, marmalade and yuzu juice, which also supply the confectioners and restaurants of Harukawa; see tōrō manjū and tai-yuzu meshi. On the winter solstice the inns of Tsukimi Onsen float whole yuzu in their baths. Geographical Indication[edit] In 2019 Tsukimi yuzu (月見ゆず) from the town of Tsukimi was registered under Japan's Geographical Indication system. Registered fruit must be grown in Tsukimi Town, harvested ripe between October and December, and meet standards for peel thickness and oil content. Producers credit the cool valley climate: Tsukimi Onsen, at 310 m, has an annual mean temperature of 13.8 °C, against 16.5 °C in Harukawa. Research[edit] The Yuzuhara Field Station of Harukawa University, a 46 ha farm opened in 1956 next to Yuzuhara Station on the Kagami Line, is the main center of yuzu research in the prefecture. With the prefectural experiment station it bred Minori Kogane and studies frost damage, low-tree training that lets older farmers harvest without ladders, and the aroma compounds of the peel. Since the 2010s researchers have also tracked the effects of warmer winters, which have pushed new plantings to higher ground in Tsukimi Town.
